items.title: Rain stops play at Santa Pod European Drag Racing Finals
Tom Pidcock, Zoe Bäckstedt, Cat Ferguson lead the line as Great Britain confirms squads for UCI Road World Championships
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
GB is one of the last major nations to announce its line-ups for the eight days of racing that begin this coming Sunday, but it has now revealed what performance director Stephen Park describes as "a highly competitive squad".

Tom Pidcock leads the line in the elite men's road race, the 27-year-old star a genuine contender in a field blown open by the absence of the reigning champion Tadej Pogačar.

Adam Yates, a decorated hilly Classics rider and a teammate of Pogačar's at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, will also enjoy a protected leadership role, while the rest of the squad is geared towards support roles.

Oscar Onley has been included after placing fifth overall at the Vuelta a España, as has a breakout star from the Spanish Grand Tour, Callum Thornley, who came within a whisker of winning the stage 18 time trial.

National road race champion Fred Wright has made the boat, as have Mark Donovan, Finlay Pickering, and James Shaw.

Ethan Hayter, who almost beat Pogačar to win the short opening time trial at the Vuelta, has also been included in the elite men's squad but only for the time trial, where Thornley will take the other of the two spots.

As for the elite women's squad, Backstedt takes aim at both the road race and the time trial as she steps up to the elite level for the first time at the World Championships. Still only 21, she pulled off the junior road race and time trial world title double in 2022, and she won the U23 time trial world title last year. Now, she steps up to lead the line at the highest level.

Backstedt is joined in the elite women's road race squad by Lauren Dickson, who has impressed in the service of Demi Vollering at FDJ United-SUEZ this season, and by the former Paris-Roubaix podium finisher Pfeiffer Georgi. Josie Nelson, Flora Perkins, and Anna Henderson round out the six-woman road race squad.

Despite being the Olympic silver medallist in the discipline, Henderson will not take the second time trial spot alongside Bäckstedt; instead that goes to a surprise selection in Anna Morris. The Welshwoman is primarily known for her exploits on the track and doesn't ride for an international road team, but was second in the national championships time trial in June and has earned a call-up to her first Road World Championships at the age of 31.

The big British prospect, Cat Ferguson returns to action after a long injury lay-off to target rainbow jerseys in the U23 ranks. Ferguson did the road race - time trial double at junior level in 2024, two years after Bäckstedt, and turned pro with Movistar the following year.

Her 2026 campaign started strongly, but she has not raced since fracturing her ankle on the opening day of the Giro d'Italia Women in late May.

In the men's U23 ranks, Ben Wiggins will ride the time trial as well as the road race, where Elliot Rowe, who was the best young rider at the recent Tour of Britain, is one to watch.

  • Ethan Hayter (time trial only)
  • Callum Thornley (road race + time trial)
  • Zoe Bäckstedt (road race + time trial)
  • Anna Morris (time trial only)

items.title: The Yankees have found a way in 2026
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
The Yankees will officially be playing baseball in October after last night’s loss by Toronto, shortly followed by New York’s own win allowing for a more raucous celebration rather than a somber one. It has not come easily for them this year, as they’ve weathered more than their fair share of blows to key players and endured lengthy slumps from others, but the man who has stood at the helm all year coasted them through to the starting line once again.

I’m not one to subscribe to the notion that managers strongly impact the game positively or negatively, but Aaron Boone has been a lightning rod for criticism throughout his tenure in New York for a whole host of reasons out of his control on top of some that he does hold some influence over, so I think it’s only fair to give him some credit for what has been an incredibly difficult season to navigate. Losing Aaron Judge to start June and not getting him back until September was a severe blow to the team, as it would’ve been at any point over the last near decade, and the offense withered without him for a long while. Unlike when he went down in 2023, however, this year’s Yankees didn’t collapse with the captain out of commission, and though they tried their hardest to make the games frustrating they managed to walk the tightrope convincingly enough to stay afloat in the standings.

You could certainly credit a large portion of that success to a stronger and deeper rotation this season compared to when they were rolling out Gerrit Cole and a bunch of bodies and I’d agree, but there’s been turmoil there too as injuries continually prevented the Yankees from lining up their five best starters in a given turn through the order. On top of that, the pitching staff as a whole was a little suspect with a bullpen that many questioned at the start of the year — for good reason as it turned out. David Bednar was unquestioned as the closer, though he struggled out of the gate, but the bridge to Bednar was rickety and swinging on frayed rope at the start of the year. Fernando Cruz was a solid option who earned some late-inning appearances, but unfortunately an elbow injury has put his season (and perhaps Yankees career) in jeopardy. Camilo Doval was the initial setup man, but he turned out to be a bust in pinstripes and there were only question marks surrounding the rest of the relief corps.

The emergence of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick forming the big three at the back of the ‘pen quite possibly is the biggest reason that this team is leading the Wild Card standings with a shot at the division still, their lock-down performances holding slim lead after slim lead and putting out fires whenever called upon having bailed out an offense that looked downright putrid for weeks. Boone has rarely leaned so heavily on a pair of arms before, but he’s fitted the two into the Scott Proctor mold and reaped the rewards for doing so while seemingly keeping them fresh enough as we enter the final stretch of the regular season.

The bullpen management has been his biggest success, but Boone and the front office have pushed the right buttons in a number of areas. The team was getting nothing out of the catcher position offensively in the first half of the year, but they surprised many by not acquiring a catcher at the Trade Deadline and instead affirming their faith in Austin Wells, who shepherded the pitchers well enough but had been absolutely dreadful with the bat. He turned around and gave them a respectable July before hitting above-average in August, and though he’s gone through another slump in September he’s still become more than respectable in the lineup again. Wells is far from the only regular they’ve been rewarded for believing in — Jazz Chisholm Jr. endured a topsy-turvy season that drew plenty of criticism after he put a goal of 50 home runs and 50 steals on his shoulders in spring. The homers never came close as he hit only six through the first two months, but Jazz has gotten close on the basepaths with 40 stolen bags this year. The option of flipping Chisholm ahead of his impending free agency was floated in trade rumors but never emerged, and instead he’s turned in a season that will end up coming close to his previous two years by fWAR.

The only real shakeup that Brian Cashman made to this roster came at the deadline, where the team traded for Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos — a pair of platoon bats, though García was the big get having led the National League in slugging when he was moved and has played accordingly since. From within they called up George Lombard Jr. and sent Anthony Volpe down to Triple-A to work on his maligned offensive capabilities while also considering new positions. Both moves paid dividends, with Lombard providing a spark and an injection of youth to the lineup while Volpe got a hero’s return on Thursday when he hit a grand slam against the Rockies and received a curtain call from the fans. I can’t imagine that when Volpe was demoted he was ever significantly in the team’s immediate plans for the rest of the year, but injuries again pressed them and their choice to finally allow Volpe the space to work on his craft has paid off with him sliding into second base in Chisholm’s absence.

There’s a dozen points where this season could’ve gone up in flames for the Yankees, but here they stand in the middle of September with a ticket to at least two guaranteed games of postseason baseball with the potential for more. The division is still within their grasp even if time is running out, and they simply can’t control how well the Rays have played. They can only handle their own business, and they’ve done a phenomenal job of doing just that this year.

items.title: Russell and Hamilton concede F1 2026 title chances as Antonelli dominates
Enric Mas' maturity and calmness allowed him to capitalise on strong form, while his GC rivals have plenty of lessons to learn from the Vuelta a España – Philippa York analysis
items.author: Philippa York
items.content:
After years of trying, the final week of the season's last Grand Tour has finally delivered satisfaction to three different riders in remarkably similar circumstances. Not that they could have been entirely certain at the start of the third week that by the end of this Vuelta a España they would be on the podium at all.

The most likely of the trio to predict success was always going to be Enric Mas, who since the exit of Tadej Pogačar on stage 8 had stepped into the role of race leader with remarkable maturity. Having finished runner-up on three other occasions, it no doubt gave him insight into how the race could be won, but having come so close before, there would have been some doubts that misfortune might rear its ugly head in the remaining days.

Movistar have a track record of messing up tactics, neglecting inter-team relationships and stifling ambitions to satisfy others’ egos – these issues were certainly in my mind while watching along.

Surprisingly, there were no tantrums or drama as the days ticked by and the pressure mounted; this remained a Movistar squad in complete agreement that the mission was to have Enric Mas in the maillot rojo at the conclusion of stage 21. Not by chance or good fortune or anything random, but by hard work, good tactical moves and believing that this was the year the Mallorcan, so often the plucky challenger, was the most complete of the GC riders.

Having watched previous editions of La Vuelta where the Spanish squad managed to remove all confidence from their best riders, it has been refreshing to see them learn from past errors and actually solidify around their team leader.

Already being the strongest climber of the GC group helped, but Mas producing a time trial performance that probably surprised even himself made the task of deciphering the two remaining mountain days so much easier. It also put more pressure on Primož Roglič and Felix Gall's shoulders, as they weren’t really fighting for the overall victory anymore; instead, they had to focus on each other.

A Grand Tour of learning for several GC contenders

For sure, Primož Roglič was going to try; the four-time champion knew how to win the overall, but the problem was the legs weren’t where he needed them to be for a spectacular reversal. However, the Slovenian has to be happy with his return from the injury that hampered his preparation in the run-up to the start in Monaco.

He showed, despite his 36 years, that he still is a force to be reckoned with and didn’t put a foot wrong in the three weeks of racing. Still ambitious, still competitive and a presence not to be dismissed.

Felix Gall, on the other hand, finished La Vuelta seemingly content with his lot, which you can’t argue with if you look at just the result. However, the manner in which Decathlon CMA CGM operated does raise several questions. Before the start, they would have immediately signed up for a podium place, understandably so, but when Pogačar left the race, the French squad didn’t seem to realise that they were competing for the overall title.

Gall lacked race craft, attacking at the wrong moments, missing moves when he ought to have been vigilant and generally accepting that he was doing rather well and that was good enough. The killer instinct Mas and Roglič possessed was absent from the Austrian. Already this season, at the Giro d’Italia, he had the opportunity to learn from Jonas Vingegaard about the art of dispatching rivals. But the lesson didn’t seem to have sunk in between the two events.

His and Decathlon’s Vuelta is a case of what might have been if they had a bit more ambition and clarity in the crucial moments. The final mountain-top finish was an example of what might have been if only Gall had committed earlier, and had he spent decent time on his TT bike, then he wouldn’t have lost so much time so needlessly.

He has the power but not the position to guarantee an acceptable performance. It might seem a harsh judgement, but all the riders he is competing with are better than him because, as he has said, he doesn’t like the discomfort of time trialling. A strange observation, considering there’s no such thing as a comfortable TT.

Richard Carapaz had a similarly average individual TT, but he countered that by being aggressive and using his experience to exploit the close marking between the top three. A bigger contrast in race craft and tactics you’ll rarely see from two teams closely matched – EF Education-EasyPost were always looking for and aware of opportunities whilst Decathlon CMA CGM retreated to defensive racing and, in the process, did a lot of the work they could have passed on to Movistar.

The French squad always blinked first when there were any hesitations, and as the race went on, everyone knew they would. Conversely, Movistar never really put a foot wrong.

For a long time it looked like Netcompany-Ineos had a rider capable of following Mas and company when they lit up the race, but ultimately Oscar Onley lacked last season's form from mid-race onwards. His TT was where it was expected to be, at just under a minute behind Roglič. However, the last two mountain stages were fatal to his podium chances. Whether it was too many setbacks, lingering effects of his early illness or a level of climbing that was a little bit too fast for him, Onley wasn’t where we thought he might be. The Vuelta demanded a degree of explosiveness, and the young Scot just didn’t have enough left by the end.

In contrast, Sepp Kuss never really entered the GC equation until the penultimate day and then jumped six places after slumbering outside the top-10 for most of the last week. This wasn’t vintage Kuss on spectacular form, though; he used his experience, tenacity and the collective strength of Visma-Lease a Bike to drag himself into the top five. This season is the second time he’s ridden all three Grand Tours, so you can excuse him for taking longer to get going and, unlike in 2023 when he won, the Dutch team were here with Wout Van Aert and Matthew Brennan to look after too.

The GC was always going to be an extra cherry on top of their sprint ambitions. They won’t be complaining after five stage wins for the young Brit and two victories and the points classification for the Belgian. Both of them were in epic form throughout.

Another Slovenian talent shines at La Vuelta

Also epic was Santiago Buitrago, who sought out the mountains classification and saw off the challenge of Van Aert but didn’t get his stage win despite being in all the right breaks. Done over by Marco Brenner in the second week and again by Eddie Dunbar in the third, at least it all turned out okay in the end, which wasn’t the case for Dunbar, who crashed on the dangerous approach to the final big climb of the race.

The race organisers will have noted the lack of respect. The Swiss TT specialist beating Callum Thornley was almost forgivable until he packed his bags and scarpered.

Someone who did need to leave early was Mattias Skjelmose. He ought to have followed Mads Pedersen’s example and gone home to recover instead of flogging himself for a GC position he never looked likely to reach. Lidl-Trek had a below-par race by their standards.

As ever, there were some surprises. Cofidis and Bryan Coquard were competitive, and it’s been a while since that happened, and Groupama-FDJ United, not to be left out, also won a bunch sprint with Bastien Tronchon – a mini French revival in a race where they are often bystanders.

Jakob Omrzel appeared on our radar, looking very much like the next Slovenian youngster to amaze everyone. Only two riders in the overall top-10 won a stage: Enric Mas and Omrzel, who finished sixth overall, pushing Onley for the white jersey. He was decidedly nonplussed by his performances – quite remarkable and reminiscent of a certain Pogacar who first showed at the Spanish Grand Tour.

Uno-X Mobility did what they always do – organised, aggressive, but it hasn’t always paid off as well as it did at this Vuelta, with Andreas Leknessund outlasting Wout van Aert in the opening week after a ridiculously hard day out, and Tobias Johannessen finishing things off in Granada whole holding off another of the new names to watch, Alessandro Romele.

And finally, to go with the feeling that this edition was a Spanish fiesta, Mikel Landa won the big mountain stage, easily the hardest day and raced until everyone finished on their knees. Landa is heading back to his roots at Euskaltel next season – tears of joy and relief in equal measure.

From being a Tadej Pogačar benefit race, the 81st Vuelta a España turned into a properly entertaining contest between riders not that far apart in ability. Enric Mas won because he had the best team, good tactics and a level of calm that let him exploit his return to top form.

items.title: Yankees prospects: Week 25 minor league recap
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
We’ve reached the final stretch, folks. One week from today, we could be completely done with minor league baseball. Hudson Valley concluded a week ago, Somerset concluded on Sunday, Tampa will conclude on Wednesday at the latest, and Scranton will need a huge week to see their season go past this coming Sunday.

As we begin to wind down the minor league recaps, we bid adieu to the 2026 Somerset Patriots while checking in on the RailRiders’ playoff push and Tampa’s journey to an FSL championship.

Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders

38-30 (75-66), 2 GB in the International League East after a 2-4 week against the Rochester Red Wings (Nationals)

+55 (+58)

Home vs. Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp (Marlins)

That’s a back-breaking week for the RailRiders’ playoff hopes. They entered the week in a dead draw with Rochester, so whoever won this series was going to have the definitive advantage heading into the final week. Almost every game could’ve gone both ways, but they’re going to really be hurting over Saturday and Sunday, blowing a 6-0 lead in the former and coming up short on a late rally in the latter. They’ll now need to pick up three games in the last week to make the playoffs.

It was a pretty meh week for the offense, with the exception of some late-week heroics by Oswaldo Cabrera (multi-homer game on Sunday) and Marco Luciano (homered in consecutive games). We also saw Duke Ellis surpass 50 stolen bases, continuing a remarkable streak of baserunning excellence. It truly is something to behold how many guys down here have major league experience and prior notoriety, and that’s not even counting Mitch Garver, who continues to be in limbo after neither the Yankees nor anyone else wanted to add him to their active roster before the September 1st deadline. Not sure what’s going on there.

As for the rotation, Alexander Cornielle drew double duty and continued his strong stretch on Monday before struggling on Sunday. Elmer Rodríguez tossed four shutout innings before getting blown up in the fifth on Friday, while Kyle Carr and Xavier Rivas continued to do their piggyback system, with the latter picking up his first Triple-A win with five solid innings. Once again, Brendan Beck was the standardbearer of the week, tossing 5.1 shutout innings to continue one of the best years by a minor league starter this season. Funny enough, the Yankees have the only two starters with a sub-3 ERA and 100 innings at the level: him and Elmer.

As you might expect from a bad week, the bullpen didn’t do its job. Eric Reyzelman and Chris Kean both tossed two scoreless innings, but the veterans weren’t as sharp, namely Justin Topa, Yerry de los Santos, and Eli Morgan.

Somerset’s season came to an end this week after going 4-2 against Hartford. They played too mediocre over the last several weeks to make a serious playoff push, and wound up playing out the string this week with a group that looked a helluva lot different than the offensive juggernaut they had on Opening Day.

We saw great finishes to the season by Core Jackson and Roderick Arias, two guys who’ve had chaotic seasons. Jackson had three different IL stints, while Arias had a nightmarish start before completely saving his prospect stock with an incredible finish. The two constants at this level all season were Jace Avina and Coby Morales. The former was incredible through the end of July but had a tough end to the season. Morales was incredibly consistent from start to finish as a 20/20 bat, having found a power stroke that eluded him early in his pro career.

On the pitching side, it’s a season of disappointment. Ben Hess only pitched 56.2 innings before going on the injured list; Cade Smith had a tumultuous and inconsistent season; and the rotation spent much of the last several weeks being heavily reliant on bullpen games. Two late call-ups really opened some eyes, though. Bryce Cunningham finished strong in what felt like a lost season for a while, and Rory Fox capped his first pro season with 7.2 scoreless innings this past week and a 3.97 ERA across 47.2 innings post-promotion.

Ultimately, there’s a bunch of players here who we could see in Scranton next year, but also a handful I’d expect to start next year in Somerset, namely Arias, Jackson, Cunningham, and Fox. We’ll see if they’re joined by some aggressive promotions lower on the farm.

Add a two-run single by Tyce Armstrong, and they had what they needed to win, even with Tippie’s ninth-inning struggles. Tyler Boudreau returned after taking a nasty comebacker last week and struck out nine in five innings, but had to settle for a no-decision in a 7-5 win to secure the sweep.

In Game 1 of the FSL Championship Series on Sunday, this dynamic offense was completely silenced aside from a Luis Escudero home run in the eighth inning. Justin West tossed five shutout innings to continue his strong second half by him, but the bullpen allowed nine runs in the final few innings. Yeesh.

items.title: Lazer Verde Keneticore helmet review: An eco-conscious model for e-bike riders
items.author: Simon Lock
items.content:
481g / 17oz (size M-L)

S-M (50-56cm) amd M-L (55-61cm)

4 out of 5

Yes

Matte Lemongrass, Matte White Stone, Matte Sage Green, Matte Fort Knox, Matte Grey Onyx

Despite the e-bike helmet being a relatively new subgenre in the world of bike apparel, there are already plenty of good options – see our best e-bike helmets guide for more of them. You probably have a list of must-haves when it comes to making a purchase: safety, comfort, and not looking daft. Sustainability credentials may or may not sway your final decision, but if you are looking for a model that looks after both your head and the planet, the Lazer Verde KinetiCore is for you.

Having used the Verde on both my 40-minute pedal-powered commute and on weekend e-bike outings for many weeks now, I can vouch for it as a comfortable, stylish option that won’t break the bank. At the time of writing, I haven’t put its safety credentials or ease of recycling to the test, but the relevant certificates and documentation back those up.

Lazer have been making helmets for over 100 years and claims to have designed the first true hardshell helmet, so it has always put technical innovation at the heart of its design.

The Verde is the latest product of this ethos, being the first to feature the brand’s EcoLoc system, which allows the helmet to be disassembled and recycled after use. In fact, 70 per cent of the helmet’s weight is made from recycled materials. There is no glue, Velcro, paint or stickers, all of which make the helmet’s production and decommissioning much less harmful to the planet.

Eco credentials in cycle kit can often read like marketing guff rather than genuinely meaningful action, but this doesn’t feel like the case with the Verde. Its closest competitor in the sustainable e-bike helmet category (admittedly a pretty niche genre) is probably the POC Myelin, however, the POC doesn’t have nearly as much certification.

The Verde comes with the essential NTA 8776 certificate, which is a Dutch standard specifically for e-bikes that rubber-stamps the helmet’s ability to perform in higher-speed collisions. It was awarded 4 out of 5 stars from Virginia Tech, so isn’t quite as safe as they come, but it’s pretty good. The helmet uses Lazer’s KinetiCore (essentially an in-house alternative to the MIPS design), which uses crumple zones rather than a separate inner shell like MIPS.

The Verde claims to provide ventilation that both offers enough inflow to keep you cool, while simultaneously keeping rain out. This is achieved by having most of the vents in the shell and the liner seemingly misaligned, which looks slightly odd at first glance.

The cradle uses Lazer's TurnSys dial adjuster, but unlike some of the brand's alternative options, there is no lateral adjustment. The strap comes with the old-school pinch-release buckle where some of the Verde’s competitors opt for a magnetic clasp, but again the design leans towards simplicity over sophistication as a way to reduce waste, and I’m here for it.

The Verde doesn’t come with a visor or the means to attach one. In terms of customisation, you might want to consider attaching Lazer’s LED light. There’s also the brand's compatible Winter Kit, which connects to the inside of the helmet to add insulation for colder commutes. Given the reduced ventilation, however, you might not need any extra warmth.

There are five matte colourways to choose from, with the Sage Green and Fort Knox particularly catching the eye. Another thing to note regarding the colour is that the plastic isn’t painted (another eco decision), it’s dyed, and has proved more resistant to scratches so far. Otherwise, the design is pretty slick and isn’t as bulky as some of its peers.

Overall, the Verde performed pretty well during test rides, which consisted of both e-bike nursery drop-offs and 40-minute, non–pedal-assisted commutes into the office. It’s probably worth noting that all of this riding was done in the south of England during the long, hot summer of 2026.

The two main things that let the Verde down are its noticeable weight and insufficient ventilation. While it feels unfair to judge it too harshly during the hottest British summer on record, for me the ventilation wasn’t sufficient for medium effort or on a warm day, and after half an hour I could feel the weight on my head – unlike my ususal helmet.

In designing the vents to keep rain out, it feels as though Lazer have sacrificed too much in the way of airflow. If you’re the sort of e-bike rider who is happy to let your battery do most of the work, then this might not be a concern, but if you’re looking for an all-rounder that you can use at the weekend on longer rides, then you might want to shop around.

In terms of weight, the M-L Verde comes in at nearly half a kilo which, given it doesn’t come with in-built smart features or a visor, feels quite weighty. Compared to the similar Smith Dispatch, it’s around 100g heavier.

Again, if you are using pedal-assist, keeping to shorter distances and riding in an upright position, this is much less of an issue. I noticed the weight far more when I was commuting head-down on my Genesis Croix de Fer compared to the rides when sat up straight on my motor-equipped Tern Quick Haul.

Having stripped the design back to make it more sustainable, there’s an unfussiness to the Verde that is quite refreshing. The TurnSys dial adjuster feels a bit primitive at first but is actually really effective and robust. The lack of lateral adjustment leaves you a bit limited when it comes to catering for ponytails or just getting a customised fit.

The straps feel a little bit dated but work well and are simple to adjust once the helmet is in place, although come with a pinch-release buckle and without any chin strap pads or the like. While the lack of glue in the manufacturing process means the shell and the liner are not inseparable and feel slightly loose on occasion, knowing this is part of the eco-friendly design put my mind at rest.

Lazer haven’t gone overboard on the padding, having sacrificed both glue and Velcro in an effort to make the helmet more recyclable. One inadvertent positive of having less padding is that when things do get a bit sweaty, is that there's less material to soak it up.

Otherwise, the overall fit was fine, even for someone not blessed with the most conventional-shaped head. Trying on helmets is not something I relish, as they usually only accentuate my Frank Sidebottom-esque aesthetic, but the Verde doesn’t look overly bulky. Even in the larger M-L sizing, the helmet doesn't look excessive.

The choice of matte colours is also very easy on the eye. I didn’t fall in love with the Lemongrass option of my test helmet, but I very much like the look of the Sage Green and Fort Knox.

Anyone who is accustomed to making climate-conscious purchasing decisions knows that they often incur something of a surcharge. The Verde feels firmly in that category, given both its weight and its stripped-back design feel like they could belong to a slightly cheaper helmet.

But for those who genuinely try and make impactful choices when buying kit, the extra outlay might feel warranted. The Verde comes in slightly cheaper than the POC Myelin (at full price) and has much greater protection certification.

The simple straps without chinstraps or magnetic clasp feel slightly outdated, not to mention out of place at this price point, but won’t ultimately have a huge impact on the important things like safety and comfort.

At £99, the Verde comes in considerably more expensive than some of the best e-bike helmets, like the Specialized Mode, which has a similar stylish design and all the safety certification you need. If you’d prefer some lighting already integrated, the Nutcase Vio comes is at a similar price but has 360-degree lighting and uses MIPS technology rather than Lazer’s KinetiCore.

If you have room in the budget, there are a number of options around the £150 mark that weigh in quite a bit lighter, have integrated lights and much improved ventilation.

Overall, the Verde is a solid and aesthetically-pleasing option that will keep your head intact should the worst happen. It also comes with the added benefit of helping you sleep better at night knowing you’re doing your bit for the environment.

The insufficient ventilation and weight of the helmet might leave you a bit hot and bothered if you’re putting in a decent amount of effort or you’re out on a warm day for more than 30 minutes, but for the average e-bike commute or school run, you should be OK. There are arguably better value helmets on the market, but that depends what price you put on sustainable design. There are also helmets that come with more bells and whistles, like integrated lights, but the simplicity of the adjustment on both the cradle and straps might suit the purists out there.

As much as an e-bike helmet purchase should fundamentally be about protecting your grey matter on the road, even the most safety-conscious of us want to look nice at the same time. The Verde is a good-looking lid that isn’t overly bulky and it comes in five great colours.

Testing scorecard and notes

Fits well although uses minimal padding and is quite heavy

Comes with the NTA 8776 but only 4 out of 5 on Virginia Tech

Not sufficient for hot days or tough rides

Sustainable, stylish and great colour options

Eco-conscious approach means minimal features

items.title: 'My good shape will come in handy with sitting on the couch' - Injury forces Mischa Bredewold out of Road World Championships
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Bredewold was taking part in the four-day race in the Ardèche region of France when she crashed on the opening stage, sustaining a minor fracture to her pelvis and an injury to her elbow. Though she managed to remount and finish the stage, 10 minutes behind the winner, a hospital visit revealed the injuries.

Her SD Worx-Protime teammate Mikayla Harvey went down in the same incident, abandoned immediately and has since been diagnosed with a concussion.

While Bredewold has since undergone successful surgery on her injuries, the Dutch cycling federation has since announced Amber Kraak will take her place on the Montreal start line.

"Went to the hospital after a crash in Ardèche tour for a few stitches, went home with a ischiopubic (pelvic) fracture and surgery on my elbow wound," Bredewold wrote in an Instagram post.

"Unexpected turn of events, and beyond disappointment. Big goals were coming with Worlds in Montreal and Worlds on the track in China, which I both felt very ready for.

"I will need some time to process this big big big disappointment and to heal up, luckily my good shape will come in handy with sitting on the couch. I’m lucky to have people around me close to my heart at a time like this.. Thanks to my lovely teammates. I’ll be back!!!!! Trust the process…"

Bredewold is an excellent all-rounder and would have proved av strong backup for Dutch team leader Demi Vollering in the Worlds road race, which will be held on Saturday, September 26 in Montreal.

Starting her career at Parkhotel Valkenburg in 2021, Bredewold joined SD Worx two years later and has bagged a total of 23 victories. Though she missed out on winning a fourth successive Classic Lorient Agglomération recently, finishing second, 2026 has been another good year for the 26-year-old.

After bagging a stage of La Vuelta Femenina, she won the opening day at Itzulia Women, defending doggedly to win the GC before taking another stage win at the Vuelta a Burgos Feminas.

items.title: Audi's shrewd choice of F2 team for its first F1 junior
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Audi's first Formula 1 junior driver Freddie Slater will join forces with defending champion team Invicta in Formula 2 in 2027.

Slater narrowly missed out on the Formula 3 title at the Madring last weekend but has had a highly impressive rookie season, living up to the promise built up by strong karting success and back-to-back titles in Italian Formula 4 and the Formula Regional European Championship.

It was that early-career success that meant he had offers from multiple F1 teams to join their junior programmes from an early age.

But much like Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Slater and his management team held off on accepting those offers too early.

At the start of this year, he accepted Audi's proposal for him to become the first driver to join its F1 driver development programme as it entered F1 in 2026.

Slater fell 14 points short of winning the F3 title, having suffered a costly mechanical failure in the Monza feature race and a nightmare Madrid title-decider that allowed chief rival Ugo Ugochukwu to take the crown instead.

Slater will now move up to F2 with Invicta, the team that has taken back-to-back championship doubles in the last two years, with Audi F1 driver Gabriel Bortoleto and McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli taking the last two drivers’ titles with it. Bortoleto and Fornaroli both also went from Trident's F3 team to Invicta's F2 team, just as Slater will.

Invicta is currently hoping to make it three out of three F2 titles this year with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, who is seven points adrift of championship leader Nikola Tsolov. Invicta itself is also just six points off Campos in the teams' title race.

F2 has added an extra feature race to its next round in Baku amid uncertainty over its current final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Slater is set to make his debut in the post-season Abu Dhabi test, although this will likely have to be rescheduled if F1 cancels its Qatar and Abu Dhabi weekends as expected. F2 could decide to join F1 if it holds its season finale at Imola in December, as is the current back-up plan. Logically the post-season F2 test would also be held there.

"The move to Formula 2 is the natural next step for Freddie, and an important new phase of his development as a driver," Audi's driver development director Allan McNish said.

"He enjoyed a strong Formula 3 season, fighting for the title until the final round - showing his speed, racecraft and progress throughout the year.

"We are very proud of what Freddie has achieved this season and how he has developed along the way. Invicta Racing has had an excellent record in recent years, and we are delighted to be working with them.

"We believe it is the ideal environment for him, and we look forward to supporting him as he takes on this new challenge in 2027."

Invicta has been the clear benchmark team during the three years of F2's current car, but the series is introducing a heavily revised version of the car from 2027.

Slater was present at the launch of the new car at Monza, telling The Race: "I think it's mega. I think it's very exciting.

"Obviously F1 has changed a lot this year so F2 kind of needs to follow suit to progress to that ladder.

"So I'm very excited to get a go behind the wheel of one and it's going to be very interesting to see what it performs like."

Slater is the first confirmed 2027 F2 driver, but he’s expected to be joined by a number of his F3 rivals, including champion Ugochukwu.

A second-place championship finish in F3 and titles in F4 and FREC mean Slater, who is yet to drive an F1 car, has more than enough points to clear the 40-point threshold for an F1 superlicence.

items.title: 'I was surprised as well' - Movistar general manager Eusebio Unzué analyses Enric Mas' unexpected but welcome victory in Vuelta a España
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
The barricades from the Vuelta a España's final stage have been cleared away in Granada now, and the water in the fountain in the Paseo del Salón boulevard where the final victory celebrations took place is no longer tinged with red dye to reflect the colour of the Vuelta leader's jersey.

But the consequences of a race won by Enric Mas in the least expected circumstances - following a crash-out by Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) - has brought a fresh Grand Tour triumph to Movistar, and will take much longer to be fully absorbed.

The 2026 Vuelta is the fifth in the history of the team co-created by Eusebio Unzué back in 1980, and its first since 2016 with Nairo Quintana. It's also Spain's first victory in its home race since 2014. Enric Mas made the podium four times, but never the top place until now.

That all changed on Sunday, when Mas, who had suffered thrombophlebitis a year ago in July and endured a miserable debut in the 2026 Giro d'Italia, was able to turn the tables on his season and his entire career by claiming his first-ever Grand Tour.

All this at 31, too. After inheriting the jersey from Pogačar on stage 8, and winning on the Alto de Aitana on stage 9, he continued outgunning or equalling his rivals on every summit finish that followed, keeping the opposition at a safe distance when riding the time trial of his life on stage 18.

The triumph for Movistar represents a massive boost for Mas, the Movistar team and Spanish cycling. As Unzué, the sport's longstanding team manager, told , the full consequences will take quite a while to sink in.

Given the strength of the lineup in Monaco, when this year's Vuelta a España began on August 22, did you feel it would be very complicated to try and win it?

No doubt about it. Anywhere where our friend Pogačar is racing, in the best of cases, a second place is what's possible. But at the same time, bad luck causes things to happen to us.

It's also true that on the stage to Castelló, [where Mas caught Pogačar at the top of the main climb and they reached the finish together], that's where he showed us the first sign that he was in really great shape. Then the bad luck Tadej suffered meant Enric was converted into the overall leader, and from that day onwards, he knew how to keep the jersey all the way to here.

And the fact that Mas had such a tough time in the Giro and then kicked off again from scratch, how much did that help him?

We're never going to know how much that did, but we do know that after what happened to him in the 2025 Tour, he was almost four or five months without riding the bike. He had to start all over again this season, he went to the Giro and he was feeling great when he started, he was very optimistic. But probably his underlying physical condition was not in the right place where he wanted it to be, and he wasn't able to do the Giro how he wanted or expected.

But he kept on training, and then you all saw that in Burgos he was already going well, and then here he was faultless. He followed the same progress curve as in other years, too, where the Vuelta and the months of August and September were his best months and then the end of the season, which is where he has his best results.

That's what we're focused on now, and we don't know how the operation that he had because of the thrombophlebitis last year has helped him, too, in the long term. The important thing is that he feels very good and I think this series of results is helping him feel more and more confident and this is the final consequence. That's also come thanks to the team, who, despite the absence of Cian [Uijtdebroeks abandoned on stage 3 - Ed.] has done a great Vuelta.

Quite a few people have been surprised that Enric has been able to handle the pressure of being the race leader, because we're talking about somebody who has had some issues with questions like descending and so on. Were you surprised as well?

Yes. I was surprised as well. He was a rider who had a really promising start to his career and, when he was very young, even making second in the 2018 Vuelta, and the expectations that surrounded him were very high. He, too, was convinced that he could handle them, but in fact, he never could.

I don't know that calendar we had for him of Tour-Vuelta-Tour-Vuelta-Tour-Vuelta etc. was … sometimes the Tour is really positive for a rider and sometimes it's a real burden of responsibility which some riders have problems overcoming and sometimes they never do. And he started to feel uncomfortable with that.

But it's also true that he's a rider with a great future ahead of him, at least two or three years and above all, I think this Vuelta and the way he's raced through it will help consolidate his feelings of self-confidence.

Old Rock'n'Rollers Never Die

Was stage 20 maybe the most complicated of all to handle, with those early attacks that led to crosswinds, your support riders ahead of the GC group in breaks and Enric isolated in the main group for a large part of the toughest day of the race?

Rather than being alone on the stage, we had riders ahead of him which we could use in the race when we thought it was necessary. He was alone for a while, but as I say, the directors played their cards very well strategically and when he needed riders, the team had them ready. And in that sense, I'm very, very satisfied with how teammates of his, who'd never had a chance to fight for a leader's jersey in a Grand Tour, rose to the occasion.

What does this mean for a team and a country with a huge tradition in Grand Tours but which has struggled to get to the very top in the last few years. Is it a timely reminder that, as the Spanish song puts it, los viejos rockeros nunca mueren - old rock'n'rollers never die?

Exactly. As you know very well, we're a team that has always had the concept of grandes corredores para las grandes vueltas - top-name riders for the biggest Tours - as one of our trademarks. That's been our reference point, ever since we started in 1980 but what has happened in the last few years, three riders - Roglič, Vingegaard and Pogačar - have won almost everything in the last six years. There's been virtually no space for anybody else. There've been a few isolated exceptions, but that's been it.

What's happened is that with the internationalisation of cycling, we've got top-name riders from all over the world. But now we're benefiting from that expansion too, as a sport that's getting more and more popular across the globe. But I always think that the countries that have always been the cycling heartlands in Europe - Belgium, Spain, Italy and France - are always going to have top-name riders for Grand Tours, too.

items.title: 'I was literally bleeding out' – Chris Froome goes into detail on the injuries that 'almost killed' him, and why he assumed everyone knew he'd retired
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Chris Froome has for the first time described in detail the injuries he sustained in a training crash in August 2025, and addressed the confusion surrounding his retirement from the sport.

Speaking to , the four-time Tour de France champion revealed that he "almost died" in the crash, and that he "almost took it as a given" that the general public knew he had retired.

At the time of the incident, a 40-year-old Chris Froome was coming to the end of a career that had seen him dominate Grand Tours between 2013 and 2018. But before he could wave goodbye on his own terms, the training ride crash put a terrifying full-stop on his career and left him in hospital with life-threatening injuries.

Given that, at the time of the incident, Froome was nearing the end of a five-year contract with Israel-Premier Tech, it was clear the crash might also end his career, though no official confirmation came until this year’s Tour de France, when Froome was asked about his status at a press event for Skoda.

"A journalist asked me, 'do you still have plans of racing?' And I was just like, 'listen, this is by no means a retirement announcement, but let me make it absolutely clear: no, no desire whatsoever to be riding my bike anymore. I'm just thankful to be alive right now," said Froome, who was speaking with at the weekend at an event hosted by Ekoï, the brand that supplies clothing and helmets to his old team, NSN Cycling.

"I almost killed myself on the bike, it was months' hospital time and medical issues, and having to take medication to try and get myself back to health again. It was really just trying to sort myself out, to be able to live a normal life again, I almost took it as a given that everyone knew I'd stopped.

"I was literally in hospital, still, through January. I crashed in August. I was in no state to be making announcements or doing PR.

"I told people when I signed my contract, I said 'this will be my last contract', so I thought it was very clear to people, even though I crashed before I was able to do an official retirement announcement."

'If the ambulance hadn't got there so quickly, I don't think I'd be here today'

Though Froome made no comment on whether he would have been physically able to have carried on racing after sustaining such catastrophic injuries, the details are shocking, and some readers might find his description upsetting.

"I almost died," Froome said, his tone reflecting the gravity of the situation. "My pericardium was open, my heart was exposed. I broke all my ribs, [they] imploded into my chest cavity.

"So I've got metal plates on each of my ribs to hold the rib cage open again, because the whole rib cage like basically collapsed, and the ribs did a lot of damage to the right lung, and one of the ribs tore open the pericardium.

"So I was literally bleeding out. The ambulance got there within, I think seven, eight minutes of my crash, if they hadn't got there so quickly, I don't think I'd be here today. So I'm extremely, extremely lucky."

One of Froome’s weekend duties with Ekoï was riding his bike, but it was a long while after his crash before he was able to get out again.

"I did get on the bike literally just for a spin, I think it was in December sometime, but I had an infection around some of the metal plates that they put on my ribs, and I had to go back into surgery again, and more tubes into my lungs," he said.

"It was only really the end of January, February that I was kind of back into it again. Slowly, just socially now, just getting out, just to clear the head and get out with friends and have a have a good time on the bike."

items.title: 2026 Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España podium finisher Felix Gall signs for Lidl-Trek for 2027
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Lidl-Trek have announced the signing of hugely talented climber and GC racer Felix Gall for 2027 in what is a major boost to their Grand Tour aspirations for next season and beyond.

The 28-year-old has just completed the Vuelta a España, where he finished third and took his second Grand Tour podium of 2026 after finishing second in the Giro d'Italia in May behind Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike). He also won a top Spanish stage race, the Vuelta a Burgos, this summer.

Lidl-Trek also announced that Gall will be joined next year by fellow Austrian and friend Gregor Mühlberger, 32. Both riders are currently with French WorldTour squad Decathlon CMA CGM.

One of the key transfer stories of 2026, Gall has signed a three-year contract through to the end of 2029, whilst Mühlberger has signed for two years, to the end of 2028.

Fifth in the Tour de France in 2025 and the winner of the toughest high mountain stage in the same race on the Col de la Loze back in 2023, Gall's double Grand Tour podium this season has seen him take a major step forward in terms of GC consistency.

His arrival at Lidl-Trek will see the team add to a strong stable of GC riders including Juan Ayuso, a former Vuelta podium finisher himself, and Mattias Skjelmose. However, it has been reported on that Tao Geoghegan Hart, the Giro d'Italia winner back in 2020, will likely be leaving Lidl-Trek at the end of the year.

Mühlberger himself has some notable GC finishes, taking 15th in the Giro d'Italia and then winning his home race, the Tour of Austria, in July. He was part of Gall's support team on the Vuelta, providing notable support on the crunch stage to Aitana, but then crashed out on stage 13, whilst running ninth overall.

"Felix has truly grown into his role as a GC leader, and it has been exciting to watch him take another step forward each season," Lidl-Trek CEO Andy Schleck said in a press release announcing the double signing.

"Since his breakthrough Tour de France in 2023, he has continued to develop his consistency, confidence and ability to perform at the highest level across three demanding weeks. In 2026, Felix has shown that he belongs among the very best, establishing himself as a genuine Grand Tour podium contender. But we believe there is still so much more to come."

“Gregor will bring a wealth of experience to the Team over the next two years, but just as importantly, he brings the qualities every team values: loyalty, commitment and a willingness to give everything for those around him.

Gall himself said after the Vuelta podium finish that he believes the next logical move for him would be to try to win a Grand Tour, but warned that it was by no means a given and considered it a massive step. He pointed out it had taken Enric Mas (Movistar), the Vuelta winner, four podium finishes before winning it outright.

A pro since 2020, with first Sunweb (now Picnic PostNL) and then Decathlon since 2022, the former Junior World Road Race champion said in the same press release announcing his signing that, "With Lidl-Trek a new chapter in my career as professional cyclist begins.

"After wonderful years and the success that came with them, it is now time for me to take the next logical step. Lidl-Trek's high standards across all aspects of modern cycling align perfectly with my own goal of continuing to develop in the best possible way."

items.title: Just bad luck? What really robbed Norris of Spanish GP win
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
There is little doubt, even from eventual winner Kimi Antonelli, that without the "insanely unlucky" timing of the virtual safety car, Lando Norris would have won the Spanish Grand Prix.

The reigning Formula 1 world champion had built up a comfortable advantage at the head of the Madring field when Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin stopped in the run off at Turn 20 as the leaders were on lap 14 of 57.

Norris was around five seconds past the pitlane entry, and well around the final corner, when race control called for a VSC to allow Stroll’s car to be recovered.

At that point it was too late for Norris to get into the pits for a change of tyres and capitalise on the reduced time loss of doing so while the field was slowed by the VSC. Meanwhile 6.5-seconds further back, Antonelli was perfectly positioned to dive in.

With the VSC remaining out as Norris toured around slowly, committed to going for his stop at the end of the following lap.

But just before he entered Turn 21, the final right hander before the pit entry, the VSC ended. It meant that, in taking his stop, Norris lost the maximum stop time of around 25 seconds – hampered further by a slow tyre change.

That dropped him to fifth behind George Russell. Despite the clear pace advantage he showed early on, Norris’s fate was sealed by two factors: tyre degradation on the hard was negligible and overtaking was nearly impossible unless there was a big tyre offset.

Had passing been on, then McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was in no doubt about what the race outcome would have been.

"I think if overtaking was possible today, we would have had Lando again in the lead because the pace advantage was significant," he said.

In the end, Norris came home third, behind Antonelli (who acknowledged he was lucky) and Max Verstappen.

While the timing of the VSC could not have been crueller in hurting Norris to the max – coming out too late for him to respond and finishing too early for him to benefit – McLaren will still analyse if it could have handled the situation better.

And there are two key questions that it will seek answers to over the coming days.

Should it have pre-empted the VSC?

With the benefit of hindsight, it is obvious to say that the best way for McLaren to have saved Norris’s Spanish GP win would have been to stop the moment the Stroll situation was developing.

While it is true that there was nothing McLaren could have done to react quicker to the VSC being triggered, as Norris was well past the pit entry when it was called, an element it does want to understand better is if there was a way to predict where things were heading.

So when it sits down at Woking to dig through the details, it will want to understand if there was enough information from the state and location of Stroll’s car to pre-empt that the situation was going to switch from a double yellow to VSC imminently.

Stroll’s car, having suffered a brake problem, had come to a halt pointing towards a gap in the barriers – but had not gone all the way through it.

Norris had been warned over the radio shortly before arriving about there being a yellow flag, but there did not seem to be any indication that this would be a serious incident.

Once Stroll had jumped out the car, race control was happy that the marshals were ready to retrieve the Aston Martin and push it through the gap.

It is when track officials are exposed on the other side of the barriers that triggers a double yellow incident being escalated to VSC.

So was this step from a double yellow to a VSC something that McLaren could have predicted?

Based on the positioning of Stroll’s car, probably not. 

There was no major damage, no debris scattered everywhere and the AMR26 was only a few metres from safety.

So it is debatable if there was enough information in the less than 20 seconds McLaren had between being aware Stroll had stopped and the chance to make a pitstop call to be convinced that this was going to trigger a caution period.

Had it opted to go for a stop, and then race control managed to deal with Stroll’s car under double yellows, McLaren would have been lambasted for throwing a win away.

As Stella later explained: "If you get it wrong, it would be extremely penalising. From the lead, you pit unnecessarily and now you lost the victory.

"I think a good rule is to respond to what is a fact, to what is the real condition of the circuit.

"But we will definitely take a look as to whether in these conditions it was just simply obvious that it would end up in a virtual safety car. I cannot answer at the moment."

But what was not known to McLaren at the time as well was that race control’s decisions about going for the VSC option was influenced by a desire to clear up debris on the track at Turn 5 as well.

Parts of carbon fibre left on the circuit at the chicane, most likely from the collision between Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz on lap 12, posed a clear risk of causing punctures and there was a desire to remove it – which would require a VSC.

So with Stroll’s car in the position it was, the decision to go for the caution was based on the double influence of the Aston Martin and the track debris at the other side of the circuit.

This also explains why there was nearly one minute between Stroll's car being behind the barriers and the VSC ending.

While pre-empting the VSC would obviously have been the right thing to do, there would have been no way for McLaren to know about all the influences race control had in its decisions – especially the Turn 5 debris.

Should McLaren have kept Norris out?

With the VSC out and Norris past the pitlane entry, there was nothing McLaren could do before he came around again.

It made a call to bring him in that lap, obviously in the hope that the VSC continued so the deficit to those who had stopped on the previous lap was equalised.

McLaren thought until the last second that the extended VSC was due to marshals being on the track, but as Norris rolled into Turn 21 the caution period ended.

Norris was 10 seconds from the pitlane entry at this point but the team committed to seeing through on its decision to stop – even though it meant it would lose the full 25s plus what it took for a tyre change.

The subsequent slow stop, which cost more time, ultimately changed little as McLaren thinks Norris would still have returned to the track behind Russell.

The obvious question to be asked here is whether McLaren should have abandoned the stop and pushed on to build up more of a gap – and then changed tyres a few laps later.

The theory is nice based on the pace early on, but the reality was that the tyre situation in the race meant it was never going to prove beneficial.

The hard that many of the cars behind had switched to had proved to be a very robust tyre, with minimal degradation and not needing too much management.

The medium, which Norris was on at this stage, was much more fragile – so after 15 laps of running would not have been in condition for him to get his head down and build up a buffer.

So while things had looked comfortable in terms of the gap to Antonelli prior to the stops, both were coming to the end of their usable tyre life.

As one rival team said about managing the different tyres: "You could drive the medium slowly, or you could go fast and they would be gone after 10 laps."

There is also a small element that, even with the VSC ending, stopping then still has advantages over one in normal racing conditions.

Norris said: "It's the fact that everyone’s kind of on colder tyres and you’re still minimising the pit loss. But the medium tyre was destroyed and the hard tyre was amazing."

As Stella explained after the race, if Norris had stayed out, the upside was minimal.

"We considered staying out," he said. "But you have to accept the fact that now you are on relatively used medium tyres and the people behind you will be on new hards. So you're never going to open a gap on people on a new hard.

"Therefore, we kind of needed to accept that that was what we should have done. It was incredibly unfortunate."

There was little else that McLaren could have done to change the outcome – as Stella ultimately concluded that his squad suffered from a paradox of being too fast.

Had its race pace not been so good, and Norris not had those six seconds over Antonelli, then he would have been in the perfect spot to dive into the pits when the VSC was called to win the race.

But F1 is not about going slower – and McLaren ultimately knows that it was just a case of wrong place, wrong time.

As Stella reflected on Sunday night: "We take it on the chin that what we could not control just played against us."

items.title: Taj Gibson announces retirement, joins Bulls coaching staff
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The second-oldest active player in basketball is no more, as OAKAAK Taj Gibson announced his retirement on Monday afternoon following his release by the New Orleans Pelicans last week. He will join the Chicago Bulls’ coaching staff under Tiago Splitter for 2026-27.

Gibson, a Brooklyn native, was selected No. 26 overall by the Bulls in 2009 out of USC. It was with Chicago that he spent the bulk of his career, debuting as an extremely old rookie at the age of 24 and growing into one of the best backup power forwards in the game.

He finished fifth in Rookie of the Year voting in 2010, fifth in Sixth Man of the Year voting in 2012, and had the best season of his career in 2013-14, where he played all 82 games and averaged 13 points, 6.8 rebounds, and 1.4 blocks in a bench role, finishing as an extremely close runner-up to Jamal Crawford for Sixth Man of the Year.

It was in Chicago that he grew close to head coach Tom Thibodeau, a connection that would pay dividends down the road. Thibs coached the Bulls from 2010-15.

Shortly after he was canned, Gibson left Chicago as the Bulls entered a rebuild. He was traded to Oklahoma City in February 2017 with Doug McDermott and a 2018 2nd for Cam Payne, Anthony Morrow, and Joffrey Lauvergne. An interesting fact here: McDermott and the Bulls’ 2018 2nd would be flipped a few months later to the Knicks for Carmelo Anthony, and that 2nd became Mitchell Robinson.

He’d slide in next to Steven Adams as the Thunder’s starting power forward for the rest of the 2016-17 season in the first year of the post-KD era, but left in the offseason when Thibs’ new team in Minnesota came calling with a two-year, $28 million pact.

It was there that Taj emerged as a full-time starter as a grizzled veteran, posting 11.5 points and 6.9 rebounds across 153 games as a Timberwolf, but when Thibs was canned, he was out the door as well.

The most relevant chapter of his career to us came when he inked a two-year, $20 million contract with the Knicks in 2019 as part of the “four PFs” offseason in the aftermath of the KD/Kyrie disaster. David Fizdale and Mike Miller would utilize the 34-year-old as more of a center for the first time in his career, using him as a mentor for Robinson. He’d play just 16.5 minutes a game, but started 56 of the 62 games he played as a shield for a young and erratic Robinson’s foul trouble.

His team option was declined for 2020-21, but we should’ve read the tea leaves as soon as Thibodeau was hired as coach that summer. After the Nova Knick 1.0 prototype (Omari Spellman) fizzled out in the first week of January, Gibson returned to fill out the depth chart behind Robinson and Nerlens Noel.

This year marked the backstretch of Gibson’s career, where his experience and mentality were significantly more valuable than his on-court contributions. He would grow into a solid role off the bench, particularly when Robinson was injured.

With the Knicks surprisingly competitive, we suddenly saw the 35-year-old put into the spotlight when Robinson was ruled out for the season, and both he and Noel were stuck as overmatched bigs against Clint Capela and the Hawks. Of the 20 career playoff starts he had, three of them came in that first round series.

He was re-signed for 2021-22 and played a similar role, this time being forced to step up into a backup role due to Noel’s long-term injury. In a frustrating season for the team, he showed a new, interesting wrinkle to his game: shooting threes.

It looked like his time in New York was over when he signed with the Wizards in 2022-23, where he played 49 games as a vet for a very young and bad team, but he’d get one more chance to play for his hometown soon enough. When Robinson suffered a seemingly season-ending ankle injury in December 2023, it was Gibson who got a non-guaranteed contract to fill his shoes.

He’d be yo-yo’d around for the rest of the year, being released in mid-January to avoid guaranteeing his contract before inking a pair of 10-day contracts later in the season, but with Robinson’s unlikely return nearing ahead of the playoffs, Gibson played his final game as a Knick on February 14, 2024, going scoreless in nine minutes.

He finished his Knicks career averaging 4.9 points and 4.4 rebounds on 56.7% from the field in 175 games (64 starts) across four seasons. From there, he continued to be the token veteran on bad teams, playing four games in March 2024 for Detroit before signing one-year deals in both Charlotte and Memphis.

He hangs it up after playing 10 games for the Grizzlies down the stretch in 2025-26 before being traded in the Jordan Hawkins deal to the Pels, who subsequently waived him.

Gibson’s spot in Knicks lore is not that of someone who had an iconic moment that will be replayed forever, but as someone who was there as a transitional piece from the bad times to the bright times. Playing for the team he likely dreamed of playing for growing up, he transitioned from a starting-caliber forward to an end-of-roster veteran, providing depth and experience.

People forget this, but Gibson is the only player aside from Julius Randle and Mitchell Robinson whose Knicks career spanned from David Fizdale to the year 2024. He was there for LolKnicks, the We Here season, and (very briefly) the Brunson revival. Championships are not entirely built by the stars that finished the job, they’re fortified by players who built the foundation.

Maybe Gibson wasn’t a true foundational piece of the rise from irrelevance to competence, but he was a constant throughout it. It’s a great hire for a young Bulls team under an inexperienced head coach in Splitter.

On Sunday night, Pro Ref confirmed that Donohue had made a mistake in allowing Erling Haaland’s goal in City’s 1-0 victory to stand when Enzo Fernández had been in an offside position.

When a VAR considers a decision such as this they start from the point at which the goal is scored and work backwards. Here, when Haaland scores, the flag is raised by the assistant referee for offside. The VAR automatically checked that on-field decision and used a semi‑automated system to show Haaland was onside. items.title: Cédrine Kerbaol boosts SD Worx-Protime’s climbing core with two-year deal at the Dutch squad
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Just hours after another rider was announced for leaving their squad, SD Worx-Protime revealed the arrival of French climber Cédrine Kerbaol, who will join at the beginning of the 2027 season.

The 25-year-old French climber, who spent two years at EF Education-Oatly, signed a two-year deal with the Dutch squad in the hope she will boost their chances of winning hilly and mountainous races, the team describing her as the "reinforcement it was looking for".

While Kerbaol is a talented climber, she is also a talented all-rounder, having a good kick and solid form in time trials. She is also an opportunistic and aggressive racer, something SD Worx believe matches their racing ethos.

"Cédrine is truly a rider after our own hearts, someone who dares to race and break up races," Sporting Director Danny Stam said in a team press release.

"In recent years, she has proven that she has reached the very top of women’s cycling. This year, she finished sixth overall in the Tour de France Femmes and second in the Tour de Suisse. In virtually every stage race she enters, she finishes in the top 10. At 25 years of age, we’re also convinced she can still take her cycling to the next level."

"This feels like the logical next step in my career,” Kerbaol said in the press release. "Every team I’ve been part of throughout my career has increasingly matched my ever-growing ambitions. At Team SD Worx-Protime, I’ve found a squad of incredibly strong riders.

"What immediately appealed to me was Danny Stam’s genuine interest in how I want to approach things myself and how the team can support me in this. I felt heard straight away.

"Before I made my decision, I spoke to Anna van der Breggen. She’s already had a brilliant career and knows exactly how to compete strongly in the general classification. Her experience as a GC rider convinced me that this is the right environment for me to develop further as a stage racer.

"I’m actually still at the very start of my career. I’ll be able to learn a lot from her and from the team to become a better stage racer."

items.title: 'Radically different scenario' - With four riders at finish, UAE Team Emirates-XRG battle through tough Vuelta a España without Tadej Pogačar
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Less than two months on from their all-conquering and record-equalling fifth triumph in the Tour de France, UAE Team Emirates-XRG reached the end of the Vuelta a España with heads held high despite the setbacks. However, they were well aware, too, that after a hugely-promising beginning, things warped for reasons beyond their control into what proved to be one of their toughest-ever Grand Tours of recent years.

Parked in the quietest part of the teams paddock before the start of stage 21, the UAE bus had well-wishers, family and friends, as well as a hefty detachment of the Guardia Civil traffic police, who wanted to share a moment with the squad. They posed for photos and had chats with management and riders.

There was also time for a group photo for UAE's management and riders, but with just four riders finishing the race of the original eight who started in Monaco - Ivo Oliveira, João Almeida, Kevin Vermarcke and Domen Novak - it was clear how much of a toll the Vuelta had taken on the team, too.

"It was a very good Vuelta but then it changed radically in the second half," Matxin said. "That started with Tadej fall, then Pablo Torres had his knee problem the next day, then Jay Vine had to leaves and we still don't know what's wrong with him. He's maybe got a virus and we've done various tests to see what is up with him.

"After that, Pavel had two heatstrokes, and we virtually obliged him to leave because he was so disoriented. We basically told him that he couldn't go on because he was feeling very out of it and it was 43 degrees [Celsius]. So that was it, we had four riders out in four days."

The situation could not have been better beforehand, Matxin said, particularly as Pogačar came from winning the Tour de France. He then went from strength to strength in the Vuelta, claiming three stages and the lead, as well as holding the top sport in the mountains classification at the point when suddenly the crash forced the Slovenian to quit early.

"Jay Vine came from winning two stages the year before, too, he always had a good relationship with the Vuelta," said Matxin, and "even then after the disaster [of Pogačar's crash] we had a tough time first with Pablo, then Jay, then Pavel.

"We kept trying with Kevin, and João, a rider who had Epstein-Barr leading to mononucleosis earlier this year although we don't know when he had it in this period and it's been a difficult time for him.

"He has gone better but not at the level we're used to, and so he's gone from finishing second behind Jonas Vingegaard and winning on the Angliru [in the 2025 Vuelta] to suffering, and just holding on as best he can. So we've just been fighting for every stage."

As for Pogačar, Matxin said that the Slovenian continues to recover at home. It was clear over a week ago that his plans regarding the fight for a third rainbow jersey and the remainder of the season had been scratched because of his injuries. But Matxin had no news, either, regarding a possible visit to Canada to the Worlds as a 'civilian', now that Urška Žigart, his partner, had been ruled out of the Worlds after refracturing her jaw in a crash over the weekend.

Following Pogačar's departure and with the team slowly getting depleted, Matxin had plenty to do himself, as the team suffered a radical alteration in its priorities. As he told , "We went from controlling breaks to trying to be the ones who were trying to escape the control of the GC teams".

The number of UAE riders in breakaways, particularly Vermaerke, showed that they were succeeding in doing that. But as Matxin said, the switch in focus made for a very different scenario, "and we have had to adapt to that".

"Kevin, for example, was a rider who had started the Vuelta along with Pavel and Jay trying to help Tadej win stages and the overall, and we've had to adapt to something different," Matxin said.

"We've gone to being totally combative, going for stage wins, all the time. It's a change of attitude from controlling breaks to trying to break the GC teams control on the breaks. That's a very different scenario."

Thirteen stages after Pogačar's untimely exit and after more and more UAE riders followed him, Matxin was keeping a close eye on the GC battle. But if Pogačar could not make it to Granada, Matxin felt that for Mas and for Spain, a win was also a long time coming.

"I've no idea who's won the last Vuelta for Spain" - [Alberto Contador in 2014 - Ed.] but Enric and Mas deserved another one, particularly a guy like Enric who's been on the Vuelta podium four times," Matxin concluded. "And I can't think of anybody who doesn't think he's a great racer."
