items.title: Six conclusions from the Vuelta a España – Mas returns Spain to glory, Van Aert at his versatile best, and the ripple effect of Pogačar's crash
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
A day on from the end of an historic 81st edition of the Vuelta a España brings the perfect chance to reflect on the drama, emotions, and great racing we saw over three weeks from Monaco all the way to Granada.

Much has changed since the riders rolled away from the iconic casino in Monaco, where anything but Tadej Pogačar winning the overall title 21 stages later was going to be a huge surprise. But that is precisely what happened.

An innocuous piece of road on stage 8 is where the Slovenian crashed out of the race, the first Grand Tour he hasn't finished in his career. And it completely changed how the remaining stages and the race for the red jersey would unfold, with an unlikely home winner stepping into the spotlight.

There are several moments from this race that will be remembered, but so too will the weather, with blistering heat in southern Spain forcing an unprecedented stage shortening in Cordoba, and completely battering much of the peloton as they scrambled to stay cool and hydrated.

With the final Grand Tour of the season behind us, the focus will now turn to the World Championships in Canada for many riders who have raced in Spain, and then the Italian Classics, building into the Autumn and end of the 2026 racing calendar.

Before moving on from the Vuelta, though, here are our six key conclusions from this historic Vuelta a España.

Enric Mas' (and Mikel Landa's) victories finally give Spain and 'traditional' Grand Tour GC countries something to cheer about again

That's because, with all due respect to Landa, at 36, his victory was something of a throwback to the previous golden era of Spanish stage cycling. After all, his previous Vuelta stage win in 2015 in Andorra came just a few months after Alberto Contador had claimed Spain's previous Grand Tour in the Giro d'Italia that year. And it was just a year, too, after Contador had won the Vuelta (in which Landa finished 28th), Spain's previous victory in its home Grand Tour to Mas in 2026.

It's true that Mas was once considered the successor to Alberto Contador, and the Spaniard's run of Vuelta podium finishes, ironically enough, only served to remind us of that 'nearly status', as they always kept Movistar in the GC picture, but never in the middle. But Mas turned pro in 2017, with his first big gesture in a Grand Tour helping Contador win his last-ever Vuelta stage on the Angliru. By that point, Landa was an already established figure, with his third place in Contador's 2015 Giro setting him up as the rider who would carry the torch for Spain once Contador had quit.

That historic status means that Landa was (and is) one of the few remaining links to an era which Mas has now provided the strongest reminder of in over a decade. That was the time when Spain, Italy, whose last winner was Vincenzo Nibali in the Giro of 2016, and France, whose last Grand Tour winner was also in the Vuelta, back in 1995, were leading figures in three-week stage racing and when their teams like Liquigas and Movistar were amongst those that counted the most in Grand Tours.

By 2011, Chris Froome and Bradley Wiggins with Sky (for whom Landa also raced, and was considered a GC favourite in the Giro) had already set the scene for other countries with less Grand Tour success in their collective palmares to make the running and so - if we all know the outcome - had Lance Armstrong in the noughties for the USA.

But thanks to Contador and Nibali, Spain (and Italy) remained reference points all the same. While Mas' victory is a major reminder of that era, racing for a team like Movistar with an enormous heritage of Grand Tour success, it's Landa who provides one of the last direct historical links.

Looking ahead, quite how long this scenario will last or what the implications are for Spanish cycling in general remains to be seen. Landa will likely have a tough time racing a Grand Tour again, barring a wildcard invitation for Euskaltel-Euskadi in the years to come to the Vuelta or (at a stretch) another Grand Tour.

Mas, at 31, can't be seen as a long-term guarantee of Grand Tour success, although Movistar are hopeful that he will continue at the same level for at least a couple more years, which will allow more young talent (take a bow, Juan Ayuso) to fill the vacuum.

But in the meantime, the success of Landa and Mas matters a great deal. It is hoped that Mas' victory will help generate some much-needed new sponsorship interest in a country which is already at risk of losing one of its flagship ProTeams, Kern Pharma, this winter. It could also help generate or revive much greater interest in the sport across all generations in Spain.

Whatever the long-term consequences, Mas' overall victory is a timely reminder that just because traditional Grand Tour countries like Italy and Spain, have been sleeping giants, they still have a lot to say in three-week stage racing.

France are already pinning their hopes on Paul Seixas to do that in the future, but Mas' success is in the here and now, and in a sport with notoriously short memory. So even if - at 31 - he does prove to be a one-GT wonder, the occasion of a lifetime was there for Mas to seize, and he took it with both hands. Hopefully Spanish cycling in general can benefit big time from its first Grand Tour success in 10 years as a result. (AF)

The Grand Tours battle against climate change continues to hang large over the sport

Gianni Vermeersch told that the hailstorms of the first week that caused one Vuelta stage to be suspended were easier to handle than the extreme heat of weeks two and three. Regardless of which was worse, both of these phenomena arguably carried the same message.

After a brutally hot Tour de France, the hailstones and rising temperatures day after day in the Vuelta, put the effects of climate change back in the narrative of a Grand Tour, yet again.

The organisers and UCI have taken what measures they can, from cancelling one stage because of the hail to shortening another because of the heat, or being much more flexible about handing over bidons of water. But there will almost certainly come a time when these solutions are insufficient.

You could already argue that these solutions are already proving inadequate. We've reached a point where riders were abandoning the Vuelta because of heat stroke, like Pavel Sivakov (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and Arthur Kluckers (Tudor). Entire teams, like Uno-X Mobility, were being told not to get into breakaways and to simply concentrate on surviving. Even two years ago, en route to Seville in extreme heat again, riders expressed their lack of enthusiasm by staging a lengthy go-slow in the first part of the course.

If we have reached the point where riders are opting not to race, you have to ask how is it possible for organisers to justify continuing holding their events in prime-time TV slots in the mid-afternoon. Even if the health question isn't critical (which it should be), at some point viewers will become frustrated that they're not actually watching a race at times, just a procession, and the viewing figures will drop as a result. That in turn could affect the whole sponsorship model of a commercially-driven sport.

The much bigger question, though, is how this will affect riders' health, rather than (in the long-term) their wallets. The consequences of going outside and engaging in full-on exercise at times when the general population is being told to stay indoors and avoid the heat are clearly not positive.

A change of timetable doesn't have to be all year round, either, only in the summer months. And it wouldn't need to be for an entire route, either, only for stages in those most affected by or at risk of hotter weather. But given the way finishes of Grand Tours seem to be happening later and later in the day, the Vuelta was a reminder that the need to review this situation is becoming critical. (AF)

Nothing affected this year's Vuelta as much as Tadej Pogačar crashing out on stage 8 while already leading the GC by a huge margin. It completely changed the complexion of how the stages after, and the race for the red jersey, played out on the road to Granada.

With no Pogačar, it meant UAE Team Emirates-XRG, the men's peloton's top team, were reduced to more of a background role, often the first team signing on at the stage starts, and fighting for breakaways to try and win another stage after their great leader had departed. While the likes of Kevin Vermaerke and last year's Vuelta runner-up João Almeida were active throughout, they were unable to take a victory, feeling the presence of a lack of Pogačar almost as much as their competitors.

While no one would wish it on him, with the Slovenian gone, it meant an almost certain race for the podium at a maximum suddenly turned into a race for the overall victory, with Enric Mas inheriting the jersey.

Now the theory for much of the cycling world is not having the sport's best rider immediately means a better race: without him dominating, the level of everyone else should, on paper, be much closer, making for a close fought GC battle and potentially more compelling race for the overall title.

That wasn't strictly how it played out on the road, with Mas – although facing several accelerations from his rivals – never really in trouble after stage 9, when he conquered Alto de Aitana to really earn his place at the top of the standings.

Felix Gall and Decathlon CMA CGM tried, but never really looked like distancing the Spaniard, and while the presence of four-time winner Primož Roglič meant that Mas' victory was not to be called certain until the end of the last mountain stage, the Slovenian never really make significant inroads, only gaining time during the stage 18 time trial. And even on that day, Red Bull were probably hoping to gain a minute more than the 33 seconds they did in Jerez.

While, yes, it was exciting in many ways to see someone new at the top, and a home Spanish rider to electrify the crowd, the racing wasn't necessarily more compelling just because the pre-race favourite wasn't there.

However, where you could massively see the benefits of a race without Pogačar was on stage 20. The crazy breakaway fight that unfolded en route to the Collado del Alguacil, where all of the top riders in the GC had at least three guys up the road as satellite riders, is a day where you easily could've seen UAE Team Emirates-XRG controlling the race for a Pogačar long-range solo.

Did any major GC changes happen to the podium? No, but the way Richard Carapaz approached the finale was some of the most thrilling racing of the season, completely lighting up almost all of the brutal climbs in Andalucia and threatening to undo the work of Mas, Roglič, and Gall to be in the positions they were.

It's hard to imagine a world where that stage plays out again as it did if the Slovenian and his usually all-consuming team were there to "ruin" it. That said, while the previous mountain days to Calar Alto and Peñas Blancas did provide similarly exciting breakaway wins to that of Mikel Landa on stage 20, the lack of GC action in those finales really points to where no Pogačar doesn't equally equal a better GC race to watch.

But again, it's likely he would have won all of the mountain days on offer in the final 13 stages, if not at least half of them, and would this have been such a great edition without the coming-of-age for his compatriot Jakob Omrzel, Eddie Dunbar's emotional comeback victory, and maybe the most popular Grand Tour win in the 2020s with Landa conquering the queen stage after the worst year of his career? The answer is clear on this occasion. (JM)

Matthew Brennan has made a breakthrough to remember

From the times of Miguel Indurain and Tony Rominger all the way through to Tadej Pogačar the Vuelta a España is often seen as the blast-off point for contenders for Grand Tour overall success. But the long line of top fast men and all-rounders who have also made Spain a major milestone prior to heading for greater things in France and Italy in Grand Tours and beyond is also a long one, and the most recent names to do that include Jasper Philipsen, Michael Matthews, Kaden Groves, John Degenkolb and Caleb Ewan.

We can now, very definitely, add Matthew Brennan to that list. His debut Grand Tour netted the Briton a staggering total of five stage victories, at 21, the youngest ever rider to do so in a single three-week stage race.

All of this creates a considerable amount of hype, but perhaps what justifies it the most is not the total number of triumphs in itself but how Brennan won those stages and on what kind of terrain.

One was uphill (stage 2), others pan-flat (stage 11 and 17), others after hard days racing through hilly terrain (stage 5). That he could win this way over three weeks is also hugely encouraging, given he'd never raced so far in his career and on such a variety of terrain. To go the distance in the toughest Vuelta on record only lends even more credibility to his bid to earn a place in the Visma line-up for the Tour de France for 2027.

His versatility further adds to that possible presence at the Edinburgh Grand Départ next July, not his fast finishes in all kinds of terrain. Brennan also proved himself a huge asset in Wout van Aert's stage wins and in the breakaways. He fought a superb two-hander with the Belgian en route to his first Vuelta stage win in Loja, and provided an extra card to play in tricky Classics-style finishes like Granada.

That clear chemistry with Van Aert and Christophe Laporte could prove invaluable in all sorts of scenarios in the Tour, be it fighting for a win or helping Jonas Vingegaard in the more technical finales. And that adaptable approach could be what tips the scales in his favour for next summer. But either way, what Brennan achieved in this year's Vuelta is one hell of a calling card. (AF)

Primož Roglič is still good enough to go with the best, him racing in 2027 would only be a plus for the peloton

Primož Roglič was spotted waving goodbye to several people at the finish of this year's Vuelta a España, so of course, one of the first questions he was asked in his press conference was whether he would ever be coming back to the Vuelta. Within that lies also the question marks over whether he will retire before 2027, or indeed continue his career on a new team, of which no concrete information has really come out as of yet.

Roglič gave an answer in his typical fashion: "Yeah, I mean maybe, you don't know in what kind of condition or shape I come to the Vuelta, just to watch or whatever a place, but we will see. It's still anyway then one year till the next Vuelta where the future will bring us."

So it remains that while the door on his career appears to be nearing closure, it is still ajar and there is a side of him that wants to continue on, in some capacity. But what this Vuelta has confirmed is that it would be a great shame if he were to stop – aside from the humour and humility he brings to the racing, Roglič is still right up there as a Grand Tour contender.

Yes, he wasn't able to overturn Enric Mas' lead and take a record fifth red jersey home, but second place after the preparation he had is quite stunning. Knocked off his bike by a driver in training on July 31, Roglič went 10 days completely off the bike and admitted that he only really took the start because it was in his adopted home of Monaco.

But as the first two weeks unfolded, it became clear that signs of the veteran's best were still in there, and while he lacked the ruthlessness and legs to take multiple stage wins and have a strong hold on the red jersey, he still played a vital role in what developed into a fascinating GC race.

When you consider the injuries he suffered and suboptimal approach into the race, it suggests that Roglič with a clean run-in to his big targets still has the capacity to perform as an elite climber and time triallist, but he will hope with everything that he can avoid another setback.

Losing Roglič to retirement would be a great loss for cycling, and for whatever team he ends up at for 2027, hopefully they can turn his final few Grand Tours into events where we see the former dominant Slovenian delivering a deserved final hurrah on the biggest stage. (JM)

Wout van Aert has long been a rider for the Grand Tours; he is also an elite one-day Classics racer, but with his versatility and three weeks to apply his talents to the Vuelta a España, we got to see the very best of the Belgian once again in Spain.

Not only did he win two stages, both from all-out brawls in the breakaway, Van Aert also played a key role in delivering Matthew Brennan to his five stage wins on debut as star lead-out rider and in chasing down any attacks that tried to catch out the young Brit.

Van Aert finished in the top 10 of nine stages this edition, and his constant efforts to get in the breakaway saw him win the green jersey, redeeming the disappointment he had suffered two years prior when wearing the exact same jersey and having crashed out of the 2024 Vuelta, but also taking home the supercombativity prize.

It's not to say Van Aert hasn't been impressive in recent Grand Tours, winning incredible stages to Siena at the Giro last year, and dropping Tadej Pogačar to win in Paris at the 2025 Tour de France, but this level of leaving his mark on almost every day throughout the race is a return the Van Aert of old between 2020 and 2023.

And it's come at the perfect time with the World Championships just around the corner. With this type of form and set to join up with Remco Evenepoel on a star-studded Belgium team, rivals of Van Aert should be worried.

Not only was he riding well in the sprints, but Van Aert delivered another epic ride from the breakaway on stage 20 to almost chase down Santiago Buitrago in the Kind of the Mountains classification, but mostly help Sepp Kuss jump from 11th to 5th overall as Visma pulled off an elite raid.

September 27 will bring his first appearance at the Worlds road race since 2023, where he was second behind Mathieu van der Poel. With an ominous showing of form and the liberation of his Paris-Roubaix win earlier in the season, it looks like the best chance for Van Aert to try and claim the rainbow jersey he has long wanted and several times already come close to capturing. (JM)

items.title: MTB Marathon World Championships: Fairytale season for Anna Weinbeer continues for Swiss rider while German Andreas Seewald secures men's title
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Both rode solo across the line in Primiero San Martino di Castrozza for the rainbow-striped jerseys, conquering the 95.2km route through the Dolomites. The elite races were held on an extended course used for the established Mythos Primiero Dolomiti Marathon MTB races, with the long course adding up to 4,000 metres of elevation gain.

Weinbeer came in as a favourite, having won the Swiss and European championships, and she dominated the Worlds' course and field of 63 riders. She broke free after the opening 25km to ride alone for 70km, posting a winning time of 5:30:54. Claudia Peretti (Italy) won the silver while Mona Mitterwallner (Switzerland) repeated for bronze.

The US duo of Melisa Rollins and Savilia Blunk rode in just over two and three minutes back, respectively, to round out the top five.

Swiss Cycling called Weinbeer's year a "fairytale season" and that was confirmed Saturday with her first rainbow stripes. In addition to the Continental and national titles, the 31-year-old also won the UCI XCM World Cup title. Last year she finished second to Kate Courtney (USA) at Worlds.

A week prior to XCM Worlds, Seewald won the German national championship for the MTB marathon discipline a second time. He used that form to rocket away from a large home Italian squad, crossing the line solo in 4:33:47. Four Italians would follow in his wake, Gioele De Cosmo and Jakob Dorigoni riding side-by-side to secure the final medals at 3:12 back, with the European MTB XCM runner-up taking the silver and Dorigoni securing bronze.

"It still feels like a dream. All the hard work was worth it," Dorigoni posted to Instagram.

"Standing on the podium at a World Championship is something I’ve always dreamed of. To make it even more special, I crossed the finish line together with my teammate Gioele De Cosmo. Sharing this moment with him was simply amazing,"

Last year's winner Keegan Swenson (USA) finished seventh, while 2025 runner-up and this year's MTB Marathon World Cup leader David Valero Serrano (Spain) was 11th.

Hector Leonardo Paez Leon (Col)

items.title: It rivals the Continental GP5000 for performance, but now costs half the price – the Michelin Power Cup TLR tyre has up to 39% off
items.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
items.content:
The holder of our best budget road tyre crown for more than two years, Michelin's Power Cup TLR easily challenges far pricier road tyres for overall performance. At almost half the retail price of the Continental GP5000 S TR, our best overall choice, it delivers matching real-world stats, speed, and value.

Right now, that incredible value is even better as you can pick up the Michelin Power Cup for just £42.95, reduced from £70 at Merlin Cycles UK.

Senior Tech Writer Will Jones praised the Michelin Power Cup's performance, noting: "I cannot say they felt faster or slower than a GP5000 or the Vittoria Corsa Pro, but matching those benchmark tyres at nearly half the price proves just how good they are."

For US shoppers, the Michelin Power Cup TLR is priced at $48.32 at Merlin Cycles US, reduced from $78.75. However, US shoppers are subject to US import taxes which typically range from 10% to 22% depending on the item's value.

This is the best Michelin Power Cup TLR price we've ever seen. It's only in the Black wall 28mm, 30mm or 32mm sizing, but really, it's a no-brainer purchase for anyone looking for one of the best road tyres at a bargain price.

The Michelin Power Cup TLR is our best budget road tyre choice. However, don't be fooled by the budget wording, because it easily matches some of its more costly rivals on performance. It's as low as $48 at Merlin Cycles US, but there is import taxes, making this Amazon deal a better option for USA Amazon Prime members.

We've tested nearly every road bike tyre on the market, and the Power Cup featured in our testing at the Silverstone sports engineering pedalling efficiency lab. Up against Grand Tour winning rubber like the Continental GP5000 S TR and the Vittoria Corsa.

There impressive performance earnt them a strong 4 out of 5 stars, and the nod as the best budget offering. We reckon the Michelin Power Cup TLR matches the GP5000's rolling resistance at a fraction of the cost. Will Jones noted: "I love these tyres, and if I wasn’t constantly swapping rubber for testing, these are where I’d spend my own money."

The Power Cup features Michelin's Tubeless Shield technology and 4x120 tpi casing, which they say makes them durable and puncture-resistant. Will was impressed with his own real-world puncture resistance testing, saying, "I’ve had three different sets of the Power Cup, some set up tubeless, some with tubes, and I've only had one puncture."

Elsewhere, review highlights included the Power Cups' grip, even though they are a totally slick tyre, free of tread or sipes (the technical term for tread). Will was happy with the performance here, saying, "I can assure you that (the slick aesthetic) doesn’t make them less grippy." However, Will did add, If you're an aggressive crit racer, cornering hard, then perhaps you’d want to consider a more well-wrapped tread option, but for most of us, I’m pretty confident in saying they’re just fine."

For tubeless users, set up here was relatively pain-free too, and Will said, "They didn’t prove overly difficult to get onto the rim, nor did they present much of a challenge to seat, either with or without sealant in."

If you've never tried a Michelin Power Cup tyre, then at this price, and with up to 39% off, now may well be the time to try them for yourself.

items.title: Edd Straw's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix F1 driver rankings
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
The inaugural Formula 1 race at the Madring was no classic - but the Spanish Grand Prix weekend as a whole did seriously test the grid.

Here's who passed with flying colours, and who was found wanting...

- Put in a mighty qualifying lap to take an unexpected pole position in what McLaren is certain wasn't the fastest car.

- Held onto the lead at the start despite the lower grip level in the pole position grid box compared to second place, and built a healthy lead in the early stages.

- Would have won without the virtual safety car being perfectly-timed to cost him the lead as he was the fastest in race conditions.

- The rear stepping out at the last corner cost him three tenths in Q3, and denied him a potential all-time great qualifying lap. That was down to him misjudging how much his mighty lap up to then impacted tyre condition, but shows he didn't deliver the maximum possible.

- Couldn't get past Verstappen in the closing stages. But considering how difficult overtaking was for everyone and how difficult Verstappen is to pass generally, that's not something he could have done much about.

Only bad luck cost him victory.

- Recovered from an alarming moment in La Monumental on his first Q2 run to put in a superb lap on his last run, "one of the best I've done", to top the midfield and reach Q3, outpacing team-mate Pierre Gasly.

- Achieved the best-possible qualifying position for an Alpine by defeating Arvid Lindblad in Q3.

- Drove a strong race to head the midfield pack, and overachieved by one place by holding off Oscar Piastri.

- Left a fraction on the table in Q3 and was the driver with the biggest deficit to his theoretical best lap at 0.204s. Not that it made any difference to his position.

- Had he been able to pass Gabriel Bortoleto, then Liam Lawson was beatable but given the overtaking challenge that's not a big negative.

Probably his best through-weekend execution in F1.

13th 11th

- Put in a good qualifying effort on his final Q2 lap, with the three-tenths gap to Bortoleto suggesting that in qualifying conditions the Haas wasn't quite at the level of the Audi.

- Made a characteristically good start and jumped to 11th ahead of the Audis, which put him 10th once Lewis Hamilton retired early.

- But for losing a place to Nico Hulkenberg in the VSC pitstops due to Haas's pit equipment not being as advanced as Audi's, he would almost certainly have scored a point.

- Ollie Bearman's self-inflicted absence from qualifying and poor grid position make comparisons difficult, but there's nothing to suggest Ocon was leaving any significant laptime on the table.

A well-executed weekend that merited a points finish in probably the eighth-best car.

- While the Red Bull was stronger in qualifying conditions than on race pace, he got close to the maximum out of the car on Saturday - even if, as for most, there was maybe a little left on the table.

- Even on a track where passing is difficult, did a good job to keep Norris behind.

- While luck assisted him in the path to second, even if he'd stayed in third without jumping Norris it would have probably been about as much as was possible.

- Given the first-corner move was always likely to lead to a chicane cut, you can argue that this led to him being behind Antonelli, who was the other beneficiary of Verstappen having to let Hamilton past.

Largely made the most of the Red Bull.

- Was clearly the faster Mercedes driver, with his pace advantage over George Russell clear-cut.

- The vast majority of his race was well-executed, showing patience when holding position while long-running Leclerc led.

- Needed luck on his side to win, as this gave him track position over Verstappen and Norris.

- The frenetic first lap featured track cuts at Turn 1 and Turn 5, which led to him being shuffled back to third.

No question about his pace, but a little untidiness.

- Despite the self-inflicted disadvantage of having to run some old-spec power unit components as a result of his Monza crash, he was just 0.005s down on Hamilton in qualifying.

- Drove a good, clean race and did what he could in his lengthy hard stint, although ultimately the car pace meant that he was always likely to finish fourth once Hamilton had retired.

- Probably left a little pace on the table in qualifying, particularly early in the lap owing to the prep laps not being perfectly executed, but as he put it, still delivered "quite a clean lap" albeit with "a few moments here and there".

No major negatives, but still didn't look at his absolute best.

- While the huge advantage over Valtteri Bottas was inflated by his team-mate being impeded by Carlos Sainz on his final lap, Perez always looked destined to be the faster Cadillac in qualifying. And he executed well, with a strong final lap.

- Drove a strong race before a water leak in the power unit led to him first slowing then retiring, having gained places to the Turn 1 incident then chased Alex Albon.

- The only real downside is that he didn't have the chance to run the second half of the race, which wasn't his fault.

A strong weekend when he was the quicker Cadillac driver.

16th 15th

- Recovered superbly from practice troubles and his FP3 mistake to put in a strong Q1 lap. Although the advantage over Sainz was infinitesimal at 0.005s, that was a big step forward.

- Williams didn't have the pace to have done any better than 16th in qualifying, especially given Albon didn't have a fresh set of softs left for Q2.

- Drove a good race in a car that didn't have the pace to do any better.

- Struggled on Friday with deployment problems that put him on the back foot and well off Sainz's pace.

- Clipping the wall early in FP3 cost him important running.

A strong weekend, with the FP3 wall-clip the one negative.

17th 17th

- Always looked like the faster Aston Martin driver throughout the weekend.

- Was able to show the strength of the car in certain corners, which was offset by time lost on the straights.

- Battled on to the finish despite deployment troubles and a front wing change after being hit by Sainz.

- He was a tenth and a half off his personal best in sector three on his final lap, which was sufficient to swing the battle for Q2 with Albon against him.

- Race problems meant he was compromised, losing significant race time.

A decent weekend, but perhaps could have got the Aston Martin into Q2.

- While qualifying wasn't maximised, it still represented a decent recovery after his FP3 off cost him his simulation.

- Probably had the stronger underlying pace of the Ferrari drivers, although didn't make the most of it.

- Crash in FP3 cost him half of that session and his qualifying simulation run, despite his best efforts to get back to the pits against the team's instructions.

- Didn't make the most of qualifying with a small error early in the lap that cost him time.

Had the pace to achieve more, but compromised Saturday then brake misfortune meant he didn't show it.

- Showed strong pace on Friday before his crash, but despite admitting to still being down on confidence in qualifying he made Q3.

- Ran ahead of Piastri in the first stint after jumping him on the opening lap.

- Managed to hold off Hulkenberg late on.

- FP2 crash at Turn 13 when the rear end gave up immediately on turn-in cost him some running on a day when he was quick, with a hangover that led to him not joining FP3 until the closing stages.

- Couldn't hold Piastri off after the McLaren driver had made his pitstop, but considering the advantage of fresh mediums there's no disgrace in that.

FP2 crash had significant consequences, but Lindblad recovered well.

11th 10th

- Won the battle of imperfect execution with his team-mate in Q2 by 0.165s.

- Made the most of starting on softs and the timing of the VSC to take a point.

- Was the slightly better Audi driver when everything is taken into account.

- There might have been a way to get past Lindblad late on, but hardly a big negative considering the difficulty of passing.

- Didn't make the most of the car in qualifying, as slipping into Q3 was possible.

A solid weekend's work, putting the Audi broadly where it should have been.

- Made an important pass on Colapinto early on, albeit having lost the place at the start.

- Stayed out on hards under the VSC, and made that strategy work decently to capitalise on Bortoleto holding up Colapinto to finish ahead of him.

- Again struggled to follow Verstappen's pace steps as qualifying progressed, ending up a respectable but disappointed 0.352s down.

- With the caveat that it's only his third outing in the Red Bull, he was very much in the group of top-team second drivers as defined by pace.

Solid but unspectacular, with an unobtrusively effective race drive.

- Was one of the few drivers to make a successful overtaking move by passing Lawson after he made his second pitstop.

- Had a clean weekend and was on the wrong side of the VSC in terms of having started on the hard tyres - although that was a deliberate choice to open up the possibility of staying out if there was an early interruption. This was closed off when Leclerc ahead did the same thing, leading to Russell stopping and then, thanks to the mediums not having the range, having to make a second pitstop.

- There was no hint of him being at Antonelli's level throughout the weekend.

- Asked a little too much of the tyres at Turn 11 on his final Q3 lap, which cost him time but he was already gradually slipping back from Antonelli prior to that.

A step back from Antonelli in terms of pace.

- Wasn't at fault for the front-wing damage on the opening lap that compromised his race.

- Managed to pass Lindblad after making his pitstop, having run the hard/medium strategy without a VSC stop.

- Simply wasn't at Norris's level in terms of pace.

- Couldn't find a way past Colapinto in the closing stages.

A lacklustre weekend.

12th 13th

- Drove a tidy long stint on hards, keeping the quicker Colapinto behind him.

- Was unlucky with the VSC timing given he had started on hards.

- Wasn't at his best in qualifying, admitting he didn't extract the maximum from the car with being a little too conservative into Turn 1 putting him on the back foot versus Hulkenberg.

- Poor start dropped him down to 15th, but that's mitigated by the fact he was on hard Pirellis.

A middling weekend, marginally worse than Hulkenberg's.

14th 12th

- Showed good pace in the race, but the timing of the VSC meant he stayed out on hards and that didn't allow him to translate it into points.

- His underlying speed was, save for when it really mattered in qualifying, where you'd expect it to be.

- Lacklustre in qualifying, expressing bafflement at a car that felt good in FP3 struggling for grip in qualifying thanks to poor tyre prep on the outlap.

- Picked up a five-second penalty added at the end of the race for speeding in the pits, which was needless although it only cost him time, not a position.

Poor qualifying defined his weekend.

19th 18th

- The 2.098s qualifying deficit to Perez was completely unrepresentative because Bottas had to rely on his first-run time, with the second ruined by traffic and the third by Sainz impeding him.

- Looked the slower Cadillac driver overall.

- Race gave him little opportunity to shine given the damage he picked up through no fault of his own.

Had bad luck in both qualifying and the race, but didn't look to be at Perez's level.

- Ran ahead of Alonso for a couple of laps early on before falling behind him approaching Turn 13.

- Brake troubles and damage from debris meant that the race comparison with Alonso doesn't mean anything.

- Had no opportunity in qualifying given a water leak prevented him setting a time in Q1, but there was nothing before that to suggest he would have been close to Alonso's pace.

- Single-lap pace ultimately wasn't a factor for Stroll given he had a 40-place grid penalty for power-unit element changes, which limited his opportunities to impress. That context significantly mitigates the negative of the fact he didn't show anything like Alonso's single-lap pace through practice.

No chance in qualifying or the race, but also no glimmers of Alonso-like pace elsewhere.

15th 14th

- Considering the damage, his race pace was respectable, but losing time behind Perez early on limited his horizons.

- Struggled in qualifying, with the 0.880s deficit to Lindblad down to Tsunoda being far happier with the car on scrubbed tyres than fresh ones. This meant he couldn't exploit the peak of the available grip and was therefore nowhere.

- Damage at the first corner from being clobbered by Sainz meant there was no opportunity to recover from a difficult qualifying.

A nothing weekend thanks to qualifying struggles and race damage.

- Showed good pace on Friday and seemed on form heading into qualifying.

- While the pitwall takes the responsibility for being oblivious to Bottas's presence and not warning Sainz, the driver always has to take a small share of the blame, even with visibility limited.

- Qualified behind Albon (by 0.005s) but pointed to poor timing of the final run and a straightline deficit as holding him back.

- Was caught out by the inevitable Turn 1 concertina at the start then compromised his race by hitting Alonso.

Pace was fine, but too many errors.

22nd (pits) 16th

- Drove a good race from the pitlane, although his two on-track passes were of the damaged Bottas and Stroll.

- Crashing heavily in FP3 after tagging the inside wall in the Turn 10/11 sweep caused a major accident - and came after a warning on Friday when he clipped the front-left at Turn 15 with less serious consequences. It also cost him qualifying.

As he said, "I have only myself to blame" for the shunt that defined his weekend.

items.title: San Marino Grand Prix MotoGP rider rankings 2026
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
The San Marino Grand Prix weekend at Misano was dominated by Spaniards - and so are our MotoGP rider rankings for the weekend. But which of the two clear standouts leads the way this time?

2nd 1st 1st

For the second weekend running the 2027 Ducati line-up monopolises the top two in these rankings - and this time Marquez gets the nod, again by the narrowest of margins.

He had claimed on Friday he would "sign right now" for a podium and that Marco Bezzecchi was the favourite - and whether that was 'mind games-y' or not, the claim did seem backed up by what was going on on track.

But a bet on the medium rear combined with another great approach to Turn 1 at the start won Marquez the sprint - and he controlled the main race after Bezzecchi's exit.

At a track which doles out a real punishment to the right side of the body - where Marquez is compromised - he was the top Ducati in every session.

7th 6th 3rd

The standards remain sky high for Acosta, who got his customary Friday crash out of the way early on and subsequently was again on another level compared to his fellow KTM riders.

He lamented losing ground in a Fermin Aldeguer battle in the sprint - in which he claimed both were doing "stupid s**t" - and was generally unhappy with the stopping performance of his RC16.

But a "disaster"-esque warm-up on Sunday was followed up by a fantastic ride in the grand prix, delivering another podium that had never felt on the cards for KTM.

3rd8th 4th

Aldeguer had a technical issue on Friday that cost him a real shot at Q2, so did it the hard way on Saturday morning - powering to third on the grid in one of his best qualifying efforts yet in MotoGP.

He got roughed up a bit on the sprint, by Acosta but particularly by Raul Fernandez, and then coped much better in the main race with the field more spread out and the pace clearly strong.

Given Misano is so demanding physically, and Aldeguer is still injury-limited (and also riding an old bike), this was a triumph of a weekend.

6th 9th 9th

Marini's best weekend of the year, the high point of it a Q2 run to a spectacular sixth on the grid - which he did admit was probably aided by yellow-flag timings and others messing up.

Never one for excessive modesty, he described himself as "every time faster than my team-mates" this weekend - and the two races bore that out.

He was "giving everything" on Sunday to keep Fabio Di Giannantonio at bay - laughing that "for sure he hates me!" given the defensive lines, though Di Giannantonio saw no issue with it and was full of praise for his friend. Ultimately, that defensive effort was for naught, a late-race vibration in the rear forcing Marini to simply drag the bike to the finish.

9th 5th 2nd

Super-fast again, the younger Marquez had performance for a front-row start and should have been in the mix to snipe a win.

A two-crash Q2, in which he was wrong-footed by adjusting to a new soft tyre after running used rubber in preceding practice, was a hammer blow to his hopes of a truly amazing result.

Still, he recovered well in both races, so well that many went away after Sunday's contest wondering whether he really should have worked his way past his brother and put himself in position to win.

5th3rd 5th

This was so nearly an almighty smash-and-grab by Martin, who went from trailing Aprilia team-mate Bezzecchi by six tenths of a second in qualifying to being in position to win the race and extend his championship lead.

Whether he would've won the race without his compartment syndrome issue is conjecture at this point - but he certainly he feels he could have, and he feels that his title charge is emboldened by this weekend, as long as he can suitably address this arm issue, through surgery or management.

There is still a very substantial single-lap question mark - 0.546s off on Friday, 0.587s off on Saturday is a losing formula - but there's something to be said for how deftly he was navigating the race circumstances this weekend.

4th 4th 7th

Di Giannantonio was pacing for a front row (or maybe even better) after three corners of his final Q2 lap, then went down in Turn 4.

But it didn't compromise his grid position too much, and that anyway didn't seem all that important to the outcome of his weekend.

Much more impactful was that early grand prix melee that dropped him into the mid-pack - with Aldeguer squeezing him to the outside kerb at Turn 1 in the inciting incident - and a subsequent brake-lever concern that limited his ability to overtake back up the order.

13th 21st 10th

Make no mistake - after the unseemly business of his stroppy back-and-forth with Yamaha at Aragon, Quartararo properly showed up at Misano.

That was easy to overlook given his most notable moment of the weekend was a clumsy fall on the sprint while trying to set up a move on Diogo Moreira - but this indirectly will have been a consequence of being the only Yamaha rider with the potential to do anything of note. Of the 11 1m31s laps delivered by Yamahas in the sprint, Quartararo was responsible for all 11.

"It's clear he has more than us this weekend," admitted team-mate Alex Rins, usually not one to acknowledge it so plainly.

Quartararo's grand prix was more muted in terms of performance, due to a need to conserve fuel - but given that he stood his ground impressively in the top 10.

10th 7th 6th

Fernandez wasn't perfect, but clearly wasn't given the best opportunities to make much of this weekend. A return of seventh and sixth in the two races is kind of the bare minimum given the level of the Aprilia, but he can't really be faulted.

He did labour a bit on Friday, with errors in crucial moments, but navigated Q1 well - including a massive "one in 15" save tucking the front at Turn 1. But in Q2 there was a "problem on both bikes", so he was well off his Q1 time and grid position-limited, conditioning both races.

An unexpected fuel-consumption problem on Sunday meant he was in the lean engine map for virtually the whole thing and never got the chance to pick off the arm-pump-limited Martin or show much of anything.

16th15th 8th

Bastianini just missed out on Friday on what would have been a weekend-transforming top-10 place. He had decided against fitting a fresh front tyre for his final time attack - which is not an unconventional decision, but in his case it proved "a big mistake".

The pace was probably there to do better (he set his fastest lap of the grand prix, and a very good one at that, on the final lap, in typical Bastianini fashion) but from 16th on the grid it was never really on the cards, and even for all these caveats there is little doubt the transcendent Acosta had much more performance.

12th 16th 14th

'The world's fastest journalist', or whatever they say, lived up to the billing this weekend by grabbing onto the back of Acosta and powering to a great Q2 appearance.

But that 'journalist' quip is increasingly more relevant. It has been a long, long while since Espargaro has raced regularly and it is showing. He "missed the aggression to overtake" on Saturday, and Sunday's race exhausted him.

He was all too keenly aware at the end that he was a 35-year-old fighting against a grid of largely 20-somethings. "My respect to Marc Marquez and Johann Zarco!" he laughed.

21st 18th 12th

The best laptime of Razgatlioglu's weekend came in the grand prix, on lap 12. If you know your MotoGP, you know this is extremely suboptimal in terms of extracting a positive result.

He said knowledge of Misano from World Superbike "did not help" here, and his one-lap pace was extremely poor, particularly in a "very bad" Q1.

But the race pace was obviously there, at a fairly high level. He was the top Yamaha on the road, in the sprint, though lost a position for track limits, then was right with Yamaha benchmark Quartararo in the grand prix - though again fell foul of track limits, even if the resulting long lap didn't actually cost him a position.

11th 10th DNF

The follow-up at Misano was more like what we all would have expected from Zarco's comeback weekend at Aragon - and even so, the actual speed was fairly decent.

Zarco navigated Friday well to land in Q2, but this was probably flattering his ultimate potential race trim. Still, he could have been much higher on the grid had he improved on his second Q2 run - and had he avoided a penalty for impeding Bezzecchi, which he acknowledged as "totally fair".

He got stuck behind a fuel-managing Quartararo on Sunday before missing his braking at Turn 8 late on and going down.

17th 20th DNF

Mir was markedly slower than usual relative to his fellow Honda riders, but this seemed to have less to do with a lack of confidence on braking he reported on Friday and more to do with some sort of unspecified ailment that increasingly bothered him over the weekend.

Suffering from a headache and with no strength, he gutted it through a fruitless sprint but had to give up very early in the main race, fearing that riding around "would only make the situation worse".

He now has medical tests to do between here and the Red Bull Ring to properly figure out his situation.

15th11th DNF

After a run of really strong form of late, Misano was largely a letdown for Moreira.

For most of the weekend, the third sector - and Curvone in particular - was the culprit, as he and LCR struggled to stabilise the Honda sufficiently in the fast right-hander.

He said after the sprint: "I told Honda, tomorrow we're cutting this corner, I don't care!" But Moreira actually made a bit of a breakthrough there in Sunday warm-up, then fell off right away on Sunday without managing to properly confirm his work.

1st 2nd DNF

This one will sting for a while.

A 37-point weekend looked on the cards for Bezzecchi after his blistering record lap in Q2 - but it turned into a nine-pointer instead, with defeat in the sprint and catastrophe in the main race.

He seemed in a real hurry to break away from Marquez and the rest of them at the start of the grand prix, but with the bike unsettled through Curvone and the subsequent Turn 12 he arrived at Turn 13 compromised and lost the front.

Forget about this being a home race or whatever. This is a monumental blow for his championship.

19th14th 11th

"Not fast enough" was Binder's summary through the weekend and at the end of it. His qualifying was "a bit s**t" and his race pace was generally underwhelming, but he did spare his KTM team any repair bills and finished in the points.

He's pacing for an inglorious, ill-fitting conclusion to his MotoGP tenure - but is at least just quietly struggling rather than properly imploding. Or is it better to burn out than to fade away (my my, hey hey)?

8th 12th 13th

Despite lacking confidence again with the Ducati GP25, Morbidelli looked notably more competitive than for most of his difficult final season in MotoGP. He gets a bit of credit for this - but it gets almost entirely offset by the fact he didn't capitalise on the opportunity.

Another instance of impeding a fellow rider - this time Bastianini on Friday - needlessly capped his Sunday potential by virtue of a long lap penalty, meaning Saturday was the best shot at a headline result.

But no such luck. He looked uncharacteristically timid in the early laps of the sprint, roughed up a bit by Moreira and then forced to spend the rest of the race shadowing the LCR Honda rider without a way past.

20th 19th DNF

Friday had looked gently encouraging but proved a mirage as Rins ultimately just didn't have all that much performance to offer this weekend - and was not happy with the bike.

He was only ever in play for some attrition-aided points on Sunday but became part of said attrition, parking up as he suffered from a "migraine and severe nausea".

18th17th DNF

A freak "cold brakes, cold tyres" crash at Rio literally something like 30 seconds into the weekend set the tone for Miller.

He just wasn't very competitive, chasing the right set-up all throughout and falling off in the grand prix as early as lap two shortly after a ding-dong battle with Zarco.

He said the bike felt improved on Sunday but "I didn't get to do bugger all on it".

14th13thDNF

Favourable track, unfavourable track, home track, foreign track, left-handers, right-handers, hard braking, high-speed - suddenly it just doesn't seem to matter at all.

This is the third time in a row (and yet only the third time this season) that Bagnaia sits lower than 20th in these rankings. He has looked all wrong since his arm-pump surgery - though he clearly seems of the opinion this is more coincidence than causation.

"It's extremely easy to see the difference between what my bike is doing compared to all the other Ducatis. Big, big difference, but difficult to understand why," Bagnaia lamented in-weekend, hitting a familiar note. He could not extract rear grip and struggled to stay on the bike, feeling "humiliated" by the experience.

The Turn 2 crash in the grand prix delivered a coup de grace to this terrible weekend - but who's to say it will be any better in Austria?

items.title: 'I expect a very hard race with big time gaps' – A UCI Gravel World Championships title defence for Florian Vermeersch in Nannup
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The winner of the 2025 UCI Gravel World Championships elite men's race, Florian Vermeersch, has decided to make the trip out to Australia to defend his world title on the gravel roads of Nannup.

The Belgian UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider won the title in the Netherlands with a solo effort of nearly 20km on the 180km course with 1,650 metres of climbing, with the victory finally coming after two years of taking the runner up slot at the event. This year he'll be lining up in prime position on Sunday October 11 and with the number one on his back on a decidedly different course, and one which is also considerably further from home.

The race in the remote location of Nannup will unfold over one lap of a 140.7km loop that is heavy on gravel and also throws in 3,625m of elevation gain across a series of climbs.

"Going to the Worlds as defending champion is a special feeling, but it doesn't put any extra pressure on me. I just love to do gravel races and when it fits my calendar. I'm always in," said Vermeersch in a release from the Australian race organisers.

"It would be awesome to be the first two-time winner but I'm aware that it’s not going to be easy. There are very strong competitors on the starting line.

"The course looks very hard and demanding so I expect a very hard race with big time gaps."

Vermeersch is one of the riders in the field that spends the vast majority of his time on the road, though he did give the jersey of the gravel world champion an outing at the Marly Gravel race in May, where he finished fourth in the race won by Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike).

This time Vermeersch will be lining up against some key gravel specialists, who were absent last year, with South Africa's Matt Beers and Keegan Swenson set to be on the start line. Their Specialized Off-road teammate – as well as The Traka 360, Unbound 200 and European Championships winner – Mads Würtz Schmidt will also be another key favourite on the start line.

The confirmed entries so far for the elite women's race on Saturday October 10 are also setting up a charged battle between the gravel specialists and riders crossing the discipline boundaries. The Dutch multi-discipline master of

Marianne Vos (Visma-Lease a Bike), who won the gravel world title in 2024, is among the confirmed starters, as is the dominant figure in the un-sanctioned world of gravel, Sofia Gomez Villafañe (Specialized Off-road).

Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Subscribers get unlimited access to exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

items.title: Everything we learned from F1's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
But that's not to say the weekend was a dud: the track proved a hit with drivers, and away from it there were significant revelations - about this year's title fight, but also involving the bid to keep one of F1's star drivers in the championship.

Here are our main takeaways from the Madring:

Hamilton's title bid is over

You may not have felt like there was a realistic Lewis Hamilton/Ferrari 2026 F1 title bid ongoing for a while (or, if you're sceptical, ever) but there was a notable change in tone from Hamilton about it after his early retirement with brake problems in Madrid.

In recent weeks his warnings to Ferrari over its management of races and its drivers had been all about how the title shot was getting more distant at best.

But when Sky Sports F1 put it to him in Madrid that Kimi Antonelli "looks hard to stop now", Hamilton pretty much congratulated his Mercedes replacement on the 2026 title.

"There's no stopping him and Mercedes this year," said Hamilton. "I think they've done a phenomenal job and they deserve it."

Which was about two steps further down that road than he really needed to go in the circumstances. The fact Hamilton went there shows that - at least in the immediate disgruntlement of his early Madrid retirement - the last title hope is now gone in his mind.

With the deficit now up to 101 points and few signs lately of Ferrari having Mercedes-beating pace, it would be hard to imagine any other scenario.

Aston Martin really needs some Honda help

It emerged at the Madring that FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been speaking to Fernando Alonso and Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll about the prospect of giving Honda some extra help to boost its recovery plan.

The Madring weekend exposed yet again that Honda is lacking - even though it is a far less power-sensitive circuit than Monza.

Alonso said "the engine was very bad today" after the race, saying he almost stalled at the pitstops because of an engine issue. He also reported the power unit was struggling to recover when he was slowing to respect blue flags.

So a boost for Honda can't come soon enough, and we know there isn't another major Honda upgrade coming until 2027.

Any such extra help - be it homologation freedoms, extra spending allowances, or specific rule changes in areas where Honda is failing to make progress - will require the support of other power unit manufacturers.

The good thing for Aston Martin Honda is that both Mercedes and Red Bull were receptive to the idea of once again assisting Honda, as its rivals did earlier this year.

Exactly how, what they may leverage in return, and where everyone stands in private, remains to be seen.

But the Madring was a stark reminder of how welcome that help would be right now.

Red Bull's car is still degrading

The mysterious 'car degradation' problems afflicting Red Bull this season aren't going away, based on both Max Verstappen and team principal Laurent Mekies' comments in Madrid.

Red Bull is still not offering any insight on precisely what the problem is, but Mekies admitted it's still there, has been for a long time, and will be for the rest of the season.

"There is an element of car performance degradation that is happening through a session and through a race," said Mekies.

"He's [Verstappen is] right in saying it's not a new issue. We are not sleeping on it. We have been trying to tackle that in different ways.

"Obviously, I consider it a complex issue, otherwise we would get to the bottom of it. But everyone is very constructive about it and tries to make small steps at the time to be able to get to the bottom of it eventually.

"We had a couple of positive steps in that regard this weekend. It will never be the full picture, but we certainly have - through pain - made progress in our understanding.

"We don't have all the solutions yet in the car, but I trust that we are on the right way. It will not be fast, so it's something that will probably take us through next year."

This wasn't the ideal Madring layout

As you may have seen, The Race revealed on Monday that three key areas of the track have been identified for improvement to increase the prospect of overtaking after a race bereft of passing.

What we've also learned is that those revisions - to the Turn 5 braking zone at the end of the first sector, the Turn 13 left-hander after La Monumental, and the tight Turn 20 - had already been proposed to the FIA before this year's race.

That they weren't implemented for its F1 debut, and are being made for 2027 instead, comes down to two factors: the complexities of track simulations, and complicated homologation processes.

The construction of the Madring was already tight, time-wise - work started in April last year - and was delayed by a wet winter in Madrid.

So, the safer option was to avoid any changes so no extra delays were built into the homologation process that could've hindered the construction work and opened the door to much bigger issues had the track not been ready in time.

In the case of the Madring, that process also required the involvement of local authorities. Consider that road, rail, and aviation stakeholders all needed to be consulted, alongside emergency officials and water, drainage, and other environmental agencies, and you can see why this was a risk-averse first race on this 'street' circuit.

But expect the Madring to look a little different when F1 returns next Autumn.

This isn't the end of Williams's 2026 pain

Williams awaits its big 2026 upgrade at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix but Alex Albon doesn’t think it will be enough to turn the team into a midfield contender.

Albon had another frustrating race in Madrid where he probably maximised the package, but still finished 15th, while Carlos Sainz retired with damage.

Albon said he was "just waiting for Baku" - but changed his tone when asked by The Race's Edd Straw what he was expecting from the step.

"We're finishing, really simply, 50 seconds behind the midfield at the minute in the race - so we're losing a second a lap more or less in the race, and it needs to be a pretty big upgrade to do it [wipe out that gap]," he said.

"All we know, it's going to be a good step, but is it going to be the full step? I'm hopeful for it, but I don't think it would be.

"Unfortunately, we said it last year, but the focus is on next year as well, and we realise we're too far back at the moment to have a couple of upgrades for this year. We need to focus on next year."

He added that the rate of development among the midfield has seen some teams bring "three or four upgrades a year" recently, and said some of those upgrades are "huge".

Alpine made a big step back to the front of that pack with its Dutch GP package, and Haas made progress with its Monza upgrade - and both teams are already in front of Williams.

Albon explained: "If you think of us in a normal year, Baku would have put us back in contention, but we have to be honest with ourselves, the speed of the development race this year is huge, and we've fallen back."

It is therefore unlikely that Williams will contend for points in Azerbaijan and add to its tally of 11 - but previous editions of that race have proven chaotic.

Gasly's Monza pole catalysed Colapinto

The elation from Pierre Gasly's pole position at Monza might have been short-lived given he was quickly consumed by faster rivals in the race, but that Saturday result did prove useful for Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto.

At Madrid, Colapinto qualified ninth and finished seventh ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri, with another great start off the line.

He was particularly pleased with his execution of the Madrid weekend - and credited it to learnings gained from Gasly's Monza pole.

"After Monza, I learned a lot of the quali of Pierre and I tried to do a step here. And I did it. And I maximised everything again," he said, when asked by The Race's Edd Straw whether this was his best F1 weekend in terms of execution.

"The quali was one of the best I've done. With very, very, very perfect laps. And putting the car in Q3 - that was always a bit tricky with the Audis going very fast here. And today, we stayed in front in the race and scored a lot of points.

"So, very happy. Again, it's extremely positive. And I'm very happy with the pace and the results."

He explained that Gasly's experience gave him useful information "on everything" in terms of qualifying execution in Madrid.

"On driving and energy management, from run to run, from Q1 to Q2 to Q3, were very clear. And yeah, I learned from that.

"Here, I was really on it in qualifying. On a very difficult track. Probably the most difficult one of the year to nail a lap. And also the most satisfying one when you do it. And both Q2 and Q3 were amazing laps."

It's happy days at Alpine, with Gasly - who was 12th after waiting until the end of the race to pit - also buoyed for Baku.

"Honestly, the pace was insane after that VSC [virtual safety car]. I think it's really positive," he claimed.

Haas is close to ending points drought

Haas hasn't scored a point since the Monaco GP in early June, but it did come very close to ending that dry spell in Madrid.

The car inconsistency issues that have plagued Haas all season weren't present here and Esteban Ocon was running 10th in the early stages.

But he was then jumped in the pitlane under the virtual safety car by Nico Hulkenberg because of an Audi pitstop that, in terms of time spent in the pitlane, was 1.133s faster than Haas's.

"We lost out on the pitstop against Audi, but I don't believe it was our team's fault; it's really the equipment that we need to improve to give them a better chance," Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu explained.

That dropped Ocon just out of the net points-paying positions, leaving him 11th at the chequered flag despite a late push.

But Ocon still felt that was an overachievement, saying "we extracted more than what the car could do" even if he was "sad at the same time because we could have got a point".

Team-mate Ollie Bearman couldn't do the same after the FP3 crash that ensured he missed qualifying, started from the pitlane and ended up 16th.

But Bearman thinks Baku will suit the upgraded Haas as it hopes to fend off an Audi team that's been slowly chipping away at Haas's points advantage in the fight for seventh in the constructors' championship.

items.title: 'I think I took last year for granted' – Oscar Onley fights through setbacks with vital lessons learnt from successful rollercoaster Vuelta a España
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Three weeks, two crashes, and one stomach bug later, Oscar Onley arrived at the finale of his first Grand Tour with Netcompany Ineos in Granada with some important lessons learned, taking sixth overall and the white jersey of Best Young Rider at the Vuelta a España after a rollercoaster race.

But it all threatened to come unstuck before he really got going at his second Vuelta, with the fourth stage to Andorra making him consider whether it was worth continuing on, having suffered stomach issues overnight.

It wasn't an easy road, but with a mixture of successes and failures across the 21 stages, Onley agreed that his fourth Grand Tour had had a bit of everything.

"That sums up pretty well. I think when I look back at where I was with the setbacks I had throughout the first two weeks, especially, then actually to still be in that GC position by the end was something I'm quite proud of," said the young Scot, speaking to after the final podium ceremony on Sunday evening.

"Especially on that Andorra stage, I got quite sick overnight, and I was really expecting to – to be honest, I was half expecting to turn off the course halfway through and ride home because, yeah, I was pretty down bad that morning, but so I'm quite happy overall."

Joining Ineos as a headline signing for 2026, Onley arrived as a big-money transfer, fresh off the back of finishing fourth at the Tour de France, and with a lot of pressure on his shoulders. He was expected to be a main leader, but struggled throughout the season with setback after setback stunting his development.

Thinking back to that Tour, in comparison to the tough road he's endured this Vuelta, Onley had gained some perspective. This gritty performance and 2026 season could prove to be more useful for his career, in the way he's had to handle the setbacks and comebacks.

"I think I took last year for granted," he said honestly, "Like I literally had no setbacks or nothing went wrong in that Tour. I think what I experienced in this Grand Tour is more probably more normal, I would say. Everyone has setbacks during a Grand Tour, and it's kind of about how you deal with them.

"The team have been really, really calm around it, and we've really made good plans on how to recover from these setbacks, especially that second crash. Initially, I didn't think it set me back much, but actually, my body didn't really react in the way I wanted it to, and it took quite a few days to really recover from that.

"So we kind of went into quite conservative mode and really tried to make the most of that, and it made a big difference when it came to well. The first goal was the TT after that, so yeah, it shows that it works."

Learning from the experience of Jack Haig

One of the key members of the roster who guided him was former Vuelta podium finisher Jack Haig, whose experience offered a calm shoulder for Onley to lean on, both in hectic finishes and in the mountains. In what was just their first race together, it wouldn't be surprising to see the Scot request the services of the Australian as he develops further as Netcompany Ineos' main GC rider.

"This was my first race with Jack, so that was also something that I wasn't sure how it would go in the beginning because obviously, to start a Grand Tour with riders you've not actually raced with is something quite unique," Onley told .

"But I feel like we, not just Jack, but the whole team in general, clicked straight away. I think from stage 2 on we were really on it, and Jack especially is someone that has been in my position going for GC before, so he understands my thoughts and how I'm feeling towards certain situations.

"I feel I was following his wheel quite a lot on the flatter days, actually, in the finals, and it made me calmer because you know he's someone that's not going to take risks and yeah he's taking it in the smoothest way, which definitely made me feel more relaxed about everything."

While Onley dropped out of the top five spot he was occupying before the final mountain stage to Collado del Alguacil on Saturday, with a long-range Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike) raid jumping him up six spots from eleventh, after the season he's had it should prove an important performance in his career.

The stage to Alto de Aitana on stage 9 was perhaps the best version of Onley we saw at this Vuelta, finishing second there behind overall winner Enric Mas, but with a more consistent run into racing in 2027, he can expect to aim much higher and back to the levels he performed at during last year's Tour.

His next race won't be in the stage racing arena, however, as for the first time this season he will be taking on a one-day race at the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, set to play a supporting role for Tom Pidcock and Adam Yates.

items.title: After tough season, Ben Healy finds rhythm and form in time for World Championships
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
After a mixed bag of a season that saw him miss the Spring Classics and hunt for form at the Tour de France, Ben Healy seems to be finding his legs just in time for the World Championships, with a strong ride at the Grand Prix de Montréal.

Healy had an unforgettable 2025 season, winning a stage of the Tour and spending a stint in the yellow jersey before finishing third in the World Championships road race in Kigali, but has struggled to climb to those heights again in 2026.

Before Sunday, he hadn't finished in the top 10 of a race since March, but a big breakaway effort at the GP de Montréal and a strong ride after he was caught saw him take eighth on the course that will host the World Championships in two weeks' time.

"It was super hard," a tired Healy told at the end of the race, having spent 52km out front.

"I think it's known as one of the hardest of the year, this race, so it's nice. I was feeling good, I gave it a go. Not to be today, but the big one is in a couple of weeks."

As well as clearly refinding his own strength after a bit of a reset over the summer, Healy's strong Sunday was helped by the efforts of his team. With teammate Michael Leonard up the road with Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) in an earlier break, the Irishman saw an opportunity to capitalise on his good legs.

"We just always wanted to be on the front foot today, and put guys up the road, and it just gives you that option if you want to take it," he said. "I could see Michael was strong, and it wasn't really the plan, but you know, when you race like that, you give yourself options, and I used that option today."

Though he was ultimately disappointed to not be able to convert his long escape into a stronger effort, Healy could say positives that his legs are good and his level is "there or thereabouts" compared to his competitors heading into this final part of the season.

"Yeah, 100%," he said when asked if he felt his form was returning at just the right moment. "I was feeling really good today, so I'm in the right place. I know the preparation's there, and the Worlds type of racing really suits me, so yeah, I'm ready."

items.title: 'The right time to take a different path' – Blanka Vas engineers early exit from SD Worx-Protime
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
There has been another shock move in the women’s transfer market, with the Hungarian champion Blanka Vas to make a mid-season switch from SD Worx-Protime to Lidl-Trek.

With a background in cyclocross and mountain bike, Vas had been marked out for greatness ever since joining the Women’s WorldTour with SD Worx mid-way through 2021.

However, after seeing her career take off with wins in the Tour de France Femmes and Giro d’Italia Women, among other major races, her 2026 season has been one to forget, featuring just 12 race days, and no racing since May.

On Monday morning, it was revealed in a coordinated announcement between SD Worx-Protime and Lidl-Trek that the 25-year-old would be making the switch between the teams, effective not from next January but from October 1, 2026.

Mid-contract switches are not unheard of for riders who race cyclocross in the winter, but while Shirin van Anrooij is leaving Lidl-Trek to join Canyon-SRAM from November 1, Blanka Vas’ transfer comes with the possibility of the Hungarian champion representing her new team on the road this calendar year, as well as in cyclocross.

"Following open and constructive discussions, both parties have concluded that the sporting ambitions they had hoped for have not been realised over the past year. The decision has therefore been taken to give Vas the opportunity to start a new chapter in her career,” read a statement from SD Worx-Protime.

The team indicated that the driving force for the parting of ways was Vas herself, with sporting director Danny Stam adding: “She has expressed a desire to explore what she can achieve with another team. We understand her position and wish her every success and happiness for the future."

Soon after, Lidl-Trek announced the arrival of Vas from October 1, on a contract that will run through 2028.

"I’ve followed her closely over the last few years and have always believed in the level she can reach,” said team boss Frank Schleck. "At Lidl–Trek, our ambition is not only to bring together the best talent, but to create an environment where riders can develop, challenge themselves and reach their full potential. We believe we can give Blanka exactly that.

"Her versatility, racing instinct and team mentality will make us stronger across the entire calendar. She has already proven her quality on the road and in cyclocross, and we’re especially excited that she’ll pull on the Lidl–Trek jersey very soon for the upcoming CX season. Blanka represents exactly the kind of ambitious, multi-discipline rider we want to build our future around.”

As for Vas herself, she was quoted in the announcements from both teams.

“This was not an easy decision, but after a number of discussions, we all felt that this was the right time to take a different path,” she said in the SD Worx press release. “I would like to thank everyone at Team SD Worx-Protime for their support, professionalism, dedication and friendship over the past 5.5 years. It is now time for a new chapter in my career.”

Soon after, in Lidl-Trek’s press release, she added: “I have very good feelings about it and can’t wait to get to know everyone in the team. I am super excited. I’m mostly looking forward to the new environment, the new challenges and everything I can learn. I’m excited to start this new chapter, get to know everyone and see what we can achieve together as a team.

“I hope I can keep improving and become a stronger rider. I’d also like to get some experience in a leadership role at some races and see how I can handle that. I think it would be a good opportunity for me to learn and grow.”
